name: North Face (Beckey-Schmidtke Route)
beta: The route begins from camp at 3,000 ft on the North Fork Nooksack River and ascends via a reconnoitered route to reach the bergschrund at 6,500 ft. From there, climbers kick steps up an 800-foot, 50-degree ice couloir on the north face, then traverse westward into a rock trough before tackling the final 1,200 feet of fourth-class rock climbing along the north arête to the summit.
overview: A dramatic and serious rock spire on the northeast side of Mount Shuksan's main massif, ringed by the Price, East Nooksack, and West Nooksack Glaciers, Nooksack Tower is one of the more committing summits in the North Cascades, with a reputation for loose rock and a demanding approach. The North Face (Beckey-Schmidtke) route is the classic line, first climbed in 1946 by Fred Beckey and Cliff Schmidtke.

current.approach: From Bellingham, exit Interstate 5 at Sunset Drive/Mount Baker exit. Drive Mount Baker Highway (Washington 542) east through the town of Glacier (last resupply for groceries) and continue 13 miles to the Nooksack River bridge. Immediately before the bridge, turn left on Hannegan Pass Road (USFS #32). Stay left at 0.5 miles, then bear right onto Nooksack Cirque Road (#34) at about 1.4 miles from highway. Continue to the washout at 2.3 miles from the highway and park at Ruth Creek (elevation 2,156 feet). Hike the abandoned road beyond the washout for two miles to the original Nooksack Cirque trailhead at 2,550 feet. River ford the Nooksack (use the log crossing at the original location noted at N48.87097 W121.61267; new logs are often swept away). Proceed up the forested mountainside east of the creek, starting up the west bank of Price Creek until finding a good log crossing. Continue to the moraine above Price Lake (3,911 feet), then hike the ridgeline between Price and East Nooksack Glaciers upward from the moraine to a rock slab bivouac spot at approximately 5,900 feet. From the bivouac, gain the glacier, traverse climber's right along the glacier to an exposed snow saddle below Nooksack Tower, then drop down and work onto the main lobe of the Price Glacier.
approach_variant_names: Ruth Creek washout, Nooksack Cirque, Price Lake moraine and the ridge to the 5,900 ft slab bivy
current.descent: Beckey and Schmidtke's 1946 descent reversed the route: an uneventful series of rappels from pitons placed in the rock wall flanking the couloir, back down to the glacier and camp. Modern parties do the same — this route is a there-and-back climb, reversed rather than continuing over the summit. From the top, downclimb/rappel the north arête and rock trough back to the head of the couloir, then make a long series of rappels (parties describe roughly ten 60m rappels) down the couloir to the snow/glacier below, building anchors as needed (slings on rock horns, occasional picket or v-thread — don't count on finding fixed gear in place or trustworthy). Where conditions allow, the lower couloir is often downclimbed instead of rappelled. From the base of the couloir, reverse the approach across the glacier/basin to the bivy, then down through Price Lake, the forested slope, and the Nooksack River flats to the Ruth Creek trailhead. Because the descent is technical, parties are frequently still on the couloir or lower approach after dark — one party describes getting back to camp roughly 21 hours after leaving it. Unlike the Price Glacier route, no car shuttle is needed — this returns to the same Ruth Creek trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: An alpine rack to three inches with extra slings for the loose terrain; double ropes for descent.
current.pro_needs: Frequent placements where the rock allows; protection can be tricky in loose sections.
bivy: Shoulder camp above Price Lake, between the Price and East Nooksack glaciers
Nooksack Cirque river bottom, below the tower

name: North Face Var. Right (Directisimo)
beta: Shares the North Face's first pitch from the notch, then on pitch 2 continues up and right to a prominent vertical crack before traversing left across the face to a large boulder — a long, wandering pitch prone to rope drag. The final pitch climbs a bolted ramp up and left to the summit. Slightly harder and more sustained than the standard North Face.
overview: A harder, more direct variation of the standard North Face, sharing the same start and lower pitch but staying direct up a steeper crack system (5.8) where the standard 5.6-5.7 line turns left, before rejoining the standard route for the final pitch to the summit.

current.approach: Drive Highway 20 to the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft), ~30 miles west of Winthrop, ~1 mile west of the Washington Pass Overlook; day-use fee or Northwest Forest/Interagency pass required. Hike the Blue Lake Trail ~1.5 miles to a small meadow, then take the climber's boot path breaking off just past a small stream, up through slabs/talus/meadow to the gully between Liberty Bell and Concord Tower (often snow-filled/icy into late June). Climb the gully to the notch between Liberty Bell and Concord Tower, where this route starts alongside the standard North Face.
approach_variant_names: Blue Lake Trail and the gully to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch
current.descent: Single-rope rappels from the summit chains: down the north face in three stages to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch, or, better, two raps down the south face to the Concord-Lexington notch, since ropes tend to stick on the north side.
current.detailed_rack: A rack to 3 inches, with several parties carrying an additional 4-inch cam for the P2 crack; bolts protect the P3 ramp finish, and rap chains are fixed at the summit.
rack: Rack to 3in (some add a #4 cam for the P2 crack)
Single dynamic rope (P3 ramp is bolt-protected; fixed rap chains at the summit)
current.pro_needs: Gear to 3 inches (some bring a 4-inch cam) covers the crack systems; expect significant rope drag on pitch 2's wandering traverse without frequent extension.
current.rope_note: Single rack to 3 inches, stoppers and slings, on a 70 m rope. Do not rack off the standard North Face's grades: this variation shares the standard route's opening 5.6 crack off the notch, then takes a sustained 5.8 crack that runs hands to off-width to chimney size where the standard line turns left at 5.6-5.7, and rejoins it for an easy low-fifth pitch to the summit. Off the top, single-rope rappels work down either face; the south face is the better choice because ropes tend to snag on the north side.

name: Northwest Couloir (Cedar Creek approach)
beta: From the Cedar Creek Trail, parties leave the trail to bushwhack toward Cedar Creek, ford it (difficulty varies greatly with flow — see Watch Out), and continue cross-country along/above the Shelokum Creek drainage to open terrain below a broad, moderately angled northwest couloir. The couloir has been climbed on foot (crampons) and descended on skis; above the couloir, roughly 800 vertical feet of dry, loose talus on the north ridge leads to the summit. A 2024 ascent found the snow "shockingly icy" and bypassed part of the slope by dropping right onto loose rock and scree.
overview: An alternative, more direct line up North Gardner's north side: a trail-less approach past a ford of Cedar Creek leads to a broad northwest-facing snow couloir that climbs directly toward the summit, finishing with a stretch of loose talus along the upper north ridge.

current.approach: From Highway 20 about 17 miles west of Winthrop, reach the Cedar Creek Trailhead (about 2,950 ft) and follow the Cedar Creek Trail before leaving it to bushwhack cross-country toward Cedar Creek; a known ford crossing (via a log in some years, a wade in others) gives access to the Shelokum Creek drainage, which is followed trail-less uphill to open meadows/snowfields below the northwest couloir.
current.descent: From the summit, talus-hop back down the north ridge to the head of the couloir, then descend the snow by ski, glissade, or plunge-step depending on conditions and party equipment — one party describes boot-skiing scree to bypass icy sections before a long glissade/buttslide lower down where the slope softens and mellows. In mid-May, loose scree beside the icy slope lets you boot-ski down and skip much of the steep hard snow; take crampons off before sliding the lower slope.
current.detailed_rack: No rope or rack is used; this is a snow/scree scramble, not a roped climb.
bivy: Cedar Creek meadow camps above the falls
Klipchuck Campground and the Highway 20 road-head campgrounds

name: Southwest Slopes / South Ridge
beta: From a backcountry camp at Gardner Meadows (or, for a combined trip with Gardner Mountain, a high bivy near Point 8487), climbers work up scree and talus into the bowl below Point 8487, then make an exposed but sub-Class-3 traverse across to the North Gardner summit block. The line is entirely off-trail cross-country travel with no fixed protection, no established cairned route, and route-finding around cliff bands required. Most parties combine it with Gardner Mountain in a single overnight or two-night trip.
overview: North Gardner Mountain (8,956 ft) is the highest point in Okanogan County and the 20th-highest peak on the Washington Bulger List (the state's 100 highest summits with 400+ ft of prominence). It sits within the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness on the east side of the Cascade Crest above the Methow Valley, joined by a high connecting ridge to 8,898 ft Gardner Mountain, 59 ft lower. The standard Southwest Slopes/South Ridge line is a long, remote scramble: roughly 10 miles of trail approach up Wolf Creek to Gardner Meadows, then off-trail travel through Wolf Creek Basin and a loose scree/snow bowl to the south ridge at Point 8,487, followed by a short final ridge walk to the true summit. Terrain is mostly Class 1-2 with a few short Class 3 steps; the crux for most parties is route-finding and about 1,400 ft of loose scree below Point 8,487, not technical climbing.

current.approach: From the Wolf Creek Trailhead (~2,950 ft, end of FS Road 5005 west of Winthrop) follow Wolf Creek Trail #527 roughly 10 miles up the Wolf Creek valley to Gardner Meadows, then continue off-trail north into Wolf Creek Basin (typical high camp ~6,200-6,400 ft) below the Gardner/North Gardner saddle. A long, multi-day approach for most parties (roughly 27 miles round trip with ~7,300 ft of gain for the full trip).
approach_variant_names: Wolf Creek Trail to Gardner Meadows
current.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line — there is no rappelling on this route. From the summit, retrace the south ridge/traverse back to Point 8,487, staying on the Class 1-2 line along or just below the crest (contour under the ridge horns rather than staying strictly on the crest). From Point 8,487, drop back into the upper basin: parties commonly plunge-step down scree, glissade remaining snow, and finish on grass back down to the Wolf Creek Basin camp/contour line (roughly 1-1.5 hrs from summit to camp for a fit party in good conditions). From the basin, reverse the off-trail contour back to Gardner Meadows and rejoin Wolf Creek Trail #527 for the long hike out to the trailhead. This is a full walk-off/downclimb — no technical rappels are involved anywhere on this route; the only technical hazard is loose scree/talus and any lingering snow on the ridge approach slopes.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is used on this route — it is climbed as an unroped Class 2-3 scramble.
current.pro_needs: None — parties do not typically place protection or use a rope on this line; it is treated as advanced scrambling terrain throughout.
bivy: High basin camp above Gardner Meadows
current.rope_note: Class 2-3 walk-up/scramble via the south ridge; no rope typically carried. Occasional Class 4 terrain possible on the ridge's west side but avoidable.

name: North Ridge
beta: From a camp at Whatcom Pass (5,210 ft), head directly south on climbers' trail/talus toward the peak. The ridge narrows and steepens with elevation; expect steep, 'Eldorado-like' snow fins with real exposure, followed by loose 3rd- and occasionally 4th-class scrambling on generally poor rock near the top. Widely considered the fastest way to the summit from either approach valley.
overview: The North Ridge is the fastest, most direct way to Whatcom Peak's summit: from Whatcom Pass you simply leave the trail and head south, gaining the peak on a moderate 3rd-class rock/scree ridge. It's a popular add-on for parties already camped at Whatcom Pass, or the descent leg of an Easy Ridge-North Ridge loop off Hannegan Pass.

current.approach: Two long approaches reach Whatcom Pass (~5,200 ft), and both are roughly comparable in mileage (~16-17 miles one-way). From the west: start at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead (end of Hannegan Pass Rd/FS-32, ~3,100 ft) and follow Trail #674 about 4 miles/2,000 ft to Hannegan Pass (~5,050-5,100 ft), then descend the far side to Boundary Camp in the Chilliwack River valley. Continue down-valley on the Chilliwack River Trail (unmaintained and rough in sections, with stretches obliterated by avalanche debris) past Copper Creek Camp and US Cabin Camp, cross the Chilliwack River by the hand-operated cable car just beyond US Cabin (or ford it), then turn up the Brush Creek Trail at its junction near mile 12 and climb past Graybeal Camp and Whatcom Camp to Whatcom Pass — a long day or more typically split over 2 days with a valley-bottom camp. From the east: hire a water taxi from Ross Lake Resort (near Diablo, off SR 20) to the Little Beaver Creek trailhead (~1,600 ft) on Ross Lake, then follow the Little Beaver Trail roughly 16 miles up-valley — passing Perry Creek Camp at 4.6 miles and Twin Rocks Camp around mile 8, then the Big Beaver Trail junction at 10.5 miles — before the final steep switchback climb through big-fir forest up to Whatcom Pass. Whichever way you arrive, from Whatcom Pass a faint, informal climbers' trail leaves the maintained trail and heads directly south, gaining the broad toe of Whatcom Peak's north ridge; the path quickly gives way to snow patches and broken rock, and route-finding means staying on the crest rather than following any marked line.
approach_variant_names: From the west: Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack River Trail and Brush Creek to Whatcom Pass
From the east: Ross Lake water taxi to Little Beaver, then 16 miles up-valley to Whatcom Pass
current.descent: This is a scramble route with no rappelling — a walk-off/downclimb via either the same ridge or a loop over the summit. Reversing the North Ridge directly is unpleasant: it's a chossy nightmare of loose, exposed 3rd-to-low-4th-class terrain in its final several hundred feet below the summit, and downclimbing it with a heavy overnight pack is considered the harder, riskier option even though it's shorter. Many parties instead descend via the South Spur side: continue over/near the summit and down the south ridge's exposed Class 3 crest to the south-facing snowfield, glissade or plunge-step down to Perfect Pass, then loop back to Whatcom Pass either via the low-orbit traverse around the peak's east side or by crossing the Whatcom Glacier when it's consolidated (treat as glacier travel — rope and crevasse-rescue gear in early season). This adds distance but trades loose downclimbing for straightforward snow. No fixed rappel anchors exist on the North Ridge itself, and rope use beyond an optional running belay on the chossiest step is not described; rappels = 0, though a party uncomfortable downclimbing the loose upper ridge could improvise a natural (rock horn/gear) anchor for a short rappel.
current.detailed_rack: No fixed protection and generally no roped rock pitches for parties comfortable soloing loose 3rd/4th class.
rack: Single 30-40m rope for short-roping/belaying exposed sections (especially on descent)
Optional light rack (0.5-2in cams, small nut set, 2 slings) only if straying onto 4th-class terrain
current.pro_needs: A light rock rack is optional insurance for less experienced parties on the final loose scrambling, but the route is normally climbed unroped on the rock.
bivy: Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass
Twin Rocks and Stillwell Camps, Little Beaver
current.rope_note: A long, exposed 3rd-class ridge accessed from Whatcom Pass; some parties rope up and belay sections, especially on descent.

name: North Ridge
beta: Starting from the North Ridge Notch, climbers ascend a trough and over unprotected 5.6 slab to gain the ridge crest, then follow 2nd- and 3rd-class ramps and corners favoring the east (left) side of the crest. A short 5.0 downclimb bypasses the final gendarme before a sustained 5.4 pitch up the summit headwall (crux moves can be linked with the final pitch on a 70m rope) finishes at the true summit.
overview: The North Ridge is a moderate, less-traveled alternative to the South Buttress: an 8-pitch, roughly 600-foot Grade III 5.7 ridge climb first done by Fred Beckey, Jim Crooks, and Ed Kenney on August 19, 1940.

current.approach: Two viable approaches. From the south (standard, same SR 20 pullout as the South Buttress, 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass): follow the South Buttress approach — creek crossing, brushy climbers' path into the meadow, up into the boulder field — but bear right/north into the basin beneath the North Ridge Notch rather than left toward the South Buttress gully. From the basin, a loose, runout pitch (5.7, PG13) gains the North Ridge Notch itself; protection is marginal (one or two small cams, narrow-head-width pieces help) and this pitch should be treated as the technical/psychological crux of the approach, not the ridge above it. From the north (longer, less common): from Rainy Pass, follow the Pacific Crest Trail into the Porcupine Creek drainage, then climb 2–3 short pitches of low 5th class to gain the North Ridge Notch from that side — a legitimate option for parties camping near Rainy Pass or combining objectives, but adds significant approach time versus the SE-basin option. Hazards: loose rock and poor pro on the 5.7 notch-gaining pitch from the south, plus the same creek-crossing and brush conditions as the South Buttress approach lower down.
approach_variant_names: The SR-20 South Buttress pullout, then bear right into the basin beneath the North Ridge Notch
Rainy Pass and Porcupine Creek into the basin northwest of the peak
current.descent: From the summit, reverse the North Ridge: mostly easy downclimbing along the ridge crest with several short rappels through the steeper fifth-class steps, followed by one longer rappel back down into the North Ridge Notch (the same notch gained on the approach). From the notch, descend via the standard South Buttress/West Ridge descent line — downclimb/simul-climb down to the first set of bolted chain rappel anchors, then continue down the same four-rappel West Ridge sequence described for the South Buttress (bolted/chain anchors, ASCA-maintained hardware, single 60m rope sufficient for each rappel), before the final downclimb/scramble through the scree bowl and boulder field back to the meadow and creek crossing. A loose-rock alternative descending the West Ridge more directly from higher on the North Ridge is also mentioned in route notes but is generally considered worse (more rockfall potential) than dropping to the notch first.
current.detailed_rack: A single rack from 0.4 to 3 inches with a set of nuts covers the route; some parties carry to a #4 for extra security. Alpine draws (about 5) with double-length slings help on the wandering ridge terrain. A 60m rope is the reported minimum; a 70m rope allows linking the final two headwall pitches.
rack: Single 60m rope minimum (70m allows linking the final two headwall pitches)
current.pro_needs: Single rack 0.4-3 in cams plus nuts; a couple of narrow micro-cams or nut placements help protect the marginal, runout notch-gaining pitch.
bivy: Klipchuck Campground, with Early Winters nearby
Cutthroat basin climbers' bivy, south side
current.rope_note: A 60 m rope is reported as the minimum. Unprotected 5.6 slab gains the ridge crest, then mostly 2nd/3rd-class ramps on the east side to a final 5.4 headwall pitch (5.7 PG13 crux is loose/runout). Descent via West Ridge with 5 rappels.

name: North Ridge
beta: First recorded climbed by Mark Bebie on September 7, 1986, who reached it by descending a couloir onto an unnamed glacier north of Primus (accessed from the North Klawatti Glacier after climbing Austera Peak the same day) and traversing to the ridge's base. The ridge took about an hour to climb once gained. It is very rarely repeated and only lightly documented; other parties have approached instead from McAllister Camp via Tricouni Peak's lower north ridge, or via a north-south Primus-Eldorado glacier traverse.
overview: A seldom-climbed, more technical alternative to the standard East Slope, first climbed by Mark Bebie in 1986. What looks like a gentle ridge from a distance turns into a jagged, loose, increasingly exposed 4th-class crest topped by a short, committing 5.6 step with no good way around it. Documented ascent/attempt information is sparse — this is a route for parties comfortable soloing loose 4th class and prepared to lead a short technical pitch far from help.

current.approach: Same Thunder Creek Trailhead approach as the East Slope route (Colonial Creek Campground on SR 20, about 6 miles up the Thunder Creek Trail to McAllister Camp, then the climbers' trail up the ridge between McAllister and Thunder Creeks to a bivy at ~6,000 ft near the toe of the Borealis Glacier) — the North Ridge is reached by traversing around the lake instead of climbing the glacier from camp.
approach_variant_names: Round to the unnamed glacier north of the peak
current.descent: Because the crux notch has no fixed anchors and downclimbing loose 4th/5th class terrain is far riskier than climbing it, parties should plan to descend via the East Ridge to Lucky Pass and down the Borealis Glacier's eastern margin, even if they climbed the North Ridge to get up.
current.detailed_rack: A light alpine rock rack (small-to-medium cams and stoppers) is sufficient for the low-5th-class climbing on the ridge's generally good but locally loose rock. Carry a rope and pickets for the approach glacier, and a rope for rappelling the ridge if retreat is needed.
rack: Small-to-mid rack: cams to 2-3in, nut set
current.pro_needs: Gear is placed sparingly on this short ridge; small cams and stoppers protect the low-5th-class sections, supplemented by natural gear (slings over blocks/horns) — it is trad-only, with no fixed/bolted protection reported.
bivy: Borealis Glacier toe / Borealis Lake high camp
Colonial Creek South Campground, Thunder Creek trailhead
McAllister Hiker Camp, Thunder Creek trail
current.rope_note: Rarely climbed, described as a jagged, loose ridge (at least 4th class terrain with a 5.6 crux); standard trad rack, helmet essential for rockfall/loose rock.

name: North Ridge
beta: Approach as for Forbidden Peak and camp at lower (5,300 ft) or upper (6,400 ft) bivy sites. From camp, navigate toward Forbidden Gully or Cat Scratch Gullies and traverse toward the notch to the right of the North Ridge. Make three to four fourth-class pitches to tower base, then climb the crux 40-foot 5.5 pitch to the tower top. For descent, make one 40-foot rappel and reverse the ridge climb.
overview: Exposed ridge climb combining three to four pitches of fourth-class scrambling with a final 40-foot 5.5 pitch to a short tower. Easily completed as a half-day climb from Boston Basin campsites.

current.approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north to Burlington, then WA-20 east through Marblemount, and turn onto Cascade River Road, following its paved-then-gravel surface about 21.7 miles to a small pullout at 3,200 ft that marks the unmaintained Boston Basin Trailhead (a different stop from the Eldorado trailhead about 2.5 miles down-road, and just before the road's end at Cascade Pass). From there a steep, unmaintained climbers' path follows the old Diamond Mine roadbed briefly before climbing hard, crossing several streams, and breaking above treeline (~5,300 ft) to reach the popular Boston Basin high camp around 6,400 ft — roughly 3-4 miles one-way with about 3,000-3,300 ft of elevation gain. From camp, West Ridge climbers continue cross-country over the glacier to a couloir that gains the ridge crest. Because Boston Basin is a high-demand cross-country camping zone in North Cascades National Park, overnight parties need a wilderness permit; a portion of peak-season (mid-May to mid-October) slots can be reserved in advance via Recreation.gov's early-access lottery, with the remainder issued as limited first-come, first-served walk-up permits. For this specific route: from Boston Basin high camp, a short approach up into the Forbidden Peak zone reaches this minor summit; North and South Ridge differ only in which side of the formation is climbed from the same camp.
approach_variant_names: Boston Basin toward the Cat Scratch gullies, then the notch right of the ridge
current.descent: From tower summit, establish anchor and rappel 40 feet. Reverse fourth-class scrambling pitches and traverse back toward notch before descending to camp.
current.detailed_rack: Very light rack. The route is 2-3 pitches of nearly level ridge that's typically simul-climbed or short-roped, then a single steeper crux step (published descriptions call it 4th class, ~50-60ft; others describe it as up to 5.5) leading to the top of a short tower, where the route ends. A small set of cams from finger-size to roughly 2in plus a handful of nuts is enough to protect the crux step and build gear anchors — there is no fixed gear or anchors on-route apart from rappel slings waiting at the descent notch.
rack: Small-to-mid rack: cams 0.3-2in, small nut set
Single 60m rope for the crux 5.5 step and ~40ft rappel
current.pro_needs: Minimal protection needed overall — most of the route is easy, low-angle ridge terrain covered with minimal or no gear (simul/short-roped), with real protection only wanted on the one steeper step. Place gear opportunistically there rather than expecting a continuous crack.
current.rope_note: Mostly 4th-class ridge scrambling (3-4 pitches) to the base of a summit tower, then a short 5.5 step and a single ~40 ft rappel to descend; 60m single rope covers the rappel and short pitch.

name: North Ridge - West Side
beta: The North Ridge - West Side is one of the primary technical routes on Molar Tooth. The route ascends via the west rib with multiple short low 5th class pitches (up to 5.4), solid granite with vertical jointing, though protection is spaced in places, and enjoyable alpine climbing despite loose rock concerns. The descent via north ridge rappels requires careful anchor placement and rope management due to potential loose rock.
overview: A moderate alpine route on Molar Tooth's north ridge featuring 2-3 low to moderate 5th class pitches up the west rib to the summit, with excellent granite climbing punctuated by loose rock hazards and quality variations.

current.approach: Two primary approaches: (1) From the Cutthroat Lake trailhead on Highway 20, hike 1.8 miles with 500 feet elevation gain to Cutthroat Lake (4,800 ft). Continue another 3.7 miles with 1,800 feet elevation gain to Cutthroat Pass (6,800 ft), then follow the ridge crest south approximately 1 mile to the base of the North Ridge. (2) From Rainy Pass North trailhead (4,875 ft) on the PCT, hike about 1.5 miles north to just before Porcupine Creek (around 5,250 ft elevation), then ascend the ridge northeast toward Molar Tooth—approximately 2 miles with 2,300 feet elevation gain. The second gully provides a cleaner approach to the base of the north ridge and west rib. From the Rainy Pass PCT trailhead the round trip is roughly 4.5 miles with about 2,500 ft of gain.
approach_variant_names: Rainy Pass, the PCT north and the ridge above Porcupine Creek
Cutthroat Lake and Cutthroat Pass
current.descent: The standard descent involves 3 rappels down the north ridge from the summit, or alternatively descend southwest with an 80-foot rappel. The granite offers good anchor possibilities through cracks and features, but careful placement is essential—test all anchors before committing weight. Be vigilant for loose blocks and flakes. Rope management is critical in low light. Once below technical terrain, descend gullies back toward the pass or PCT.
current.detailed_rack: Bring complete trad rack with cams 0.5-3 inches, stoppers/nuts, and hexes. Protection on the technical pitches is spaced, so use the vertical jointing where it offers placements. Consider extra quickdraws (10-12 total) and locking carabiners for belays. The pitches are moderate in length, with a lower-angle slab where placements are far apart.
rack: Cordelette, extra tat webbing for anchor replacement
current.pro_needs: Natural rock protection via cracks and vertical jointing. Placements are spaced in places, notably on the lower-angle slab pitch. Test all anchors before committing weight and avoid placing protection in weathered sections. Expect runout stretches between pieces rather than continuous protection.
bivy: Cutthroat Lake basin, outside the quarter-mile closure
current.rope_note: Molar Tooth North Ridge/West Side: low 5th class terrain with complex route-finding and exposure; a leader may not find much protection. Descent via 3 rappels off the north ridge — some fixed anchors present but sparse traffic means bring gear to replace old tat.

name: Cloudy Peak Traverse (South Ridge)
beta: A ridge-crest link between Cloudy Peak and North Star: from Cloudy Pass, scramble the ridge up to Cloudy Peak with expanding views toward Glacier Peak, Eldorado, and Buckner, on rock that is reasonably solid Class 4 with an option to keep it at Class 3. From Cloudy Peak, lose elevation and cross talus slopes to reach North Star, finishing on the same lichen-slicked Class 3-4 summit step as the standard route. Most parties descend directly toward the Cloudy Pass Trail (rejoining it around 6,300 ft) rather than re-climbing Cloudy Peak.
overview: A harder alternative approached from the west: gain the crest at Cloudy Pass, follow the ridge over Cloudy Peak (7,915 ft), then descend and cross talus to North Star's summit block via the same short, exposed Class 3-4 step used by the East Route.

current.approach: Approach as for the East Route to Lyman Lake: either from Lake Chelan via Lucerne, Holden Village and the Railroad Creek trail, or from the Chiwawa River side via Phelps Creek, over Spider Gap and down past the Upper Lyman Lakes. Both ways have been closed in recent seasons, the Lucerne side by storm-damaged roads and the Chiwawa side by wildfire and road closures, so check current Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest closures before planning. From Lower Lyman Lake follow Trail #1256 west through forest and meadows to Cloudy Pass (6,440 ft), and gain the ridge crest there to start the traverse.
current.descent: From the North Star summit, downclimb the summit step, then make a direct beeline across talus toward the Cloudy Pass Trail, intersecting it at about 6,300 ft; follow meadows and interconnected granite slabs roughly 1.5 miles back to Cloudy Pass/Lyman Lake basin.
current.detailed_rack: Unroped scramble; no technical rock gear is documented as necessary, though some parties may choose a rope for the exposed Class 4 sections in poor conditions.
current.pro_needs: None reported; no fixed protection.
bivy: Phelps Creek Campground and the Chiwawa River road campgrounds

name: East Route
beta: From a camp at Lyman Lakes, leave the trail and hike cross-country across open meadow, then up talus and scree (Class 2) on the south side of the mountain, with the final push to the summit on looser, steeper Class 2-3 rock. The peak is commonly combined with adjacent Cloudy Peak (about 0.9 mi away) from the same basin camp.
overview: North Star Mountain sits immediately west of Bonanza Peak in the Glacier Peak Wilderness, above the Railroad Creek and Lyman Lakes basins. No maintained trail reaches the summit; the standard route climbs the peak's south side above Lyman Lake. Curiously, USGS survey crews swapped this peak's name with Bonanza Peak's on the original 1904 topographic map, and the mix-up stuck.

current.approach: Standard approach is via Holden Village: Lady of the Lake ferry from Chelan or Fields Point Landing to Lucerne, shuttle to Holden, then roughly 8 miles up the Railroad Creek Trail to Lyman Lake. Forest Road 8301 and the Lucerne commercial dock are closed under Forest Service order 06-17-05-26-04, in effect January 28, 2026 through December 31, 2027, after December 2025 storm damage — leaving the longer Phelps Creek Trailhead approach over Spider Gap (roughly 11–12 miles one-way, glacier travel with ice axe required), itself closed through October 31, 2026 by the Little Giant Fire closure (Forest Service order 06-17-07-2026-40) and reached only over closed road (Forest Service order 06-17-07-2026-11, through December 31, 2027).
approach_variant_names: Lyman Lakes basin to the south flank
Phelps Creek over Spider Gap
current.descent: Reverse the south-side talus and scree back down to the Lyman Lake basin.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed for the standard scramble.
current.pro_needs: None — this is an unroped scramble. The main terrain concern is the permanent snowfield/moat near 7,000 ft on the Spider Gap approach, which some parties treat with an ice axe for self-arrest.
bivy: Phelps Creek Campground and the Chiwawa River road campgrounds
current.rope_note: Class 2-3 talus/scree scramble in the Glacier Peak Wilderness (Lyman Lake/Cloudy Pass area); no rope typically needed.

name: North Tower Ridge Route
beta: A wonderful alpine rock climb with great exposure and views. The route offers generally solid protection with the crux featuring a wide flaring chimney and off-width section requiring careful gear placement. First three pitches establish the ridge; crux pitch (P4) is 5.7-5.8 in a chimney; final pitches are 4th class scrambling to the tower summit.
overview: An excellent six-pitch alpine climb on the North Tower ascending mostly quality granite rock on the right side of Tiffany's north face, with crack climbing, chimneys, and ridge scrambling.

current.approach: From Tiffany Springs Campground (6,760 ft), hike trail #373 east past Tiffany Lake to Honeymoon Pass (7,150 ft, ~45 minutes). From the pass, either traverse south on the grassy east slope to the small cirque at the base of the North Face (7,360 ft) and climb the boulder field to the base of the climb (7,600 ft), or hike the trail on the north side of the ridge toward Little Tiffany Lake and drop down to the base from above (~30 minutes). Three driving approaches reach the Tiffany Springs trailhead: via Conconully/North Fork Salmon Creek and FR 39 (~21 mi, ~1 hr, rough road, 4WD recommended); via the South Fork/Baldy Pass (~30.6 mi, ~2 hr, 2WD-passable gravel); or via the Methow Valley (~26.5 mi, ~1 hr, 2WD gravel). An alternate trailhead at Freezeout Pass (via East Chewuch Rd/FR 37/FR 39 from Winthrop) also accesses the area and does not require a Northwest Forest Pass.
approach_variant_names: Tiffany Springs Campground and trail #373 over Honeymoon Pass, then the east slope traverse
current.descent: From the summit, descend the northwest ridge (mostly 3rd class scrambling) to approximately 8,000 feet, then contour northeast toward Little Tiffany Lake, picking up the northeast ridge trail that descends to Honeymoon Pass. Total descent time approximately 1.5-2 hours depending on snow coverage and group speed.
current.detailed_rack: Medium traditional rack: small stoppers from sizes 0-2, full range of cams from #00 to #4 (especially #2, #3, #4), extra-long slings (2-3) for chimney protection, 60-meter rope for single-pitch belays or simul-climbing on 4th class terrain.
rack: 2-3 extra-long slings for chimney protection, plus 4-6 shoulder slings
current.pro_needs: The route features reasonable protection on most pitches with solid rock quality. The crux pitch requires careful gear placement in a wide chimney and off-width section with tricky placements. Standard rack management and knowledge of crack climbing placement essential.
bivy: Tiffany Lake and Little Tiffany Lake
The talus and benches below the north face
current.rope_note: 650ft alpine rock tower on generally excellent granite; single 60m rope for occasional belays/short raps off the tower. No confirmed fixed rap anchors — carry rap tat.

name: West Ridge
beta: The West Ridge is the standard and by far the most popular route on North Twin Sister. After a long logging-road and trail approach to treeline near Dailey Prairie, the route follows the ridge crest (keeping to climber's right of the crest on the lower ridge and moving to climber's left near the false summits, to avoid the hardest moves) past two named rock features — the 'Obelisk' and the 'Cockscomb' — with a notch around 6,300 ft that bypasses a cliff band where the crest is blocked. Most of the climbing is class 3 on excellent, high-friction rock with frequent holds; a handful of class 4 (and, on the crest itself, occasional class 5) moves are encountered, and some parties rope up for a short M1b mixed step on a variation start. Multiple false summits complicate routefinding near the top. Descent is either back down the ridge or, early season, a steep glissade down snow on the north face.
overview: North Twin Sister (6,644 ft) is the second-highest and most-visited summit of the Twin Sisters Range, a striking massif of dunite (an ultramafic, olivine-rich mantle rock) about 10 miles southwest of Mount Baker. Dunite is exposed at the surface in only a handful of places worldwide, and here it weathers to a reddish-orange rind while staying grippy, sandpaper-textured stone underneath - the reason the West Ridge has a reputation as some of the best rock scrambling in the state. A small glacier clings to the peak's northeast slopes. Both Twin Sisters summits lie inside the Mount Baker Wilderness, but the approach roads lie outside the national forest, crossing private timberland whose access policy has shifted repeatedly over the decades.

current.approach: Via Mosquito Lake Road (off SR 542 east of Deming) to a bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack River, then Forest Road 38; park at the gate and continue roughly 5-6 miles with about 2,000-2,500 ft of gain on private-timberland logging roads (commonly covered by mountain bike) to reach the West Ridge climbers' path, which climbs through timber onto the ridge crest.
current.descent: Reverse the West Ridge to the approach; the friction rock makes downclimbing straightforward. In early season (roughly late May into mid-July), many parties instead glissade a long, steep snowfield on the north slope and traverse back to rejoin the West Ridge trail near 4,600 ft.
current.detailed_rack: Not a roped rock route for most parties. A handful of parties bring a light rack and a short rope for the optional M1b mixed variation start or for the class 5 moves near the Cockscomb if climbing with less-experienced partners.
rack: Optional light rack: a few small cams/nuts for the M1b mixed variation start or Class 5 crest moves
Webbing, quick-links/rap rings for rap stations
70m half rope, harness, belay device, prusik (carried by parties tackling the harder options)
current.pro_needs: Protection needs are minimal on the standard class 3-4 line; a light rack (a few cams/nuts and slings) covers the short M1b variation start or any roped class 5 moves near the Cockscomb for parties who choose to belay them.
bivy: Dailey Prairie road end (staging and bike stash, not a camp)
Col between the Twins and the Sisters Glacier margin
current.rope_note: Class 3-4 ridge scramble, ~2000ft; trip reports show parties carrying a 70m half rope, harness, belay device, and prusik for harder sections/short raps, plus ice axe/crampons in early-season snow.

name: Northeast Face Direct
beta: Lower pitches climb a rubble-covered class 4 gully into a snow couloir that steepens past 65 degrees with overhanging chalkstones near its top; the crux is two 5.6 pitches around the 'duolith,' a loose 30-foot granite tower split by a 3-foot crack, climbed on sparse protection (one 80-meter pitch protected by a single piece) before easier class 3-4 terrain leads up the north ridge crest to the summit.
overview: Rarely-repeated alpine rock route on Mount Formidable's northeast face above the heavily crevassed Formidable Glacier in the North Cascades; first climbed in 2002, with a documented second ascent not until 2013.

current.approach: Mount Formidable is a deep objective on the Ptarmigan Traverse, reached from the Cascade Pass Trailhead at the end of the Cascade River Road. Take the maintained trail to Cascade Pass, then leave it and work across the Mixup flank on boot path, talus and snow, up the Cache Glacier to Cache Col, and down the far side to camp at Kool-Aid Lake. From the lake continue south past Art's Knoll and cross the Red Ledge, then follow a rough path over meadow, snow and talus and drop several hundred feet to the bench on the Middle Cascade Glacier between its two icefalls. Cross the bench to the foot of the Formidable Glacier below the northeast face. Allow a full day or more from the car to Kool-Aid Lake and about three hours from camp to the base of the face. The descent is the South Route, back over the Spider-Formidable col and across the Middle Cascade Glacier and Red Ledge to camp. This is a multi-day glaciated objective that needs glacier travel skills.
approach_variant_names: Cascade Pass, the traverse corridor to the Red Ledge, and the Formidable Glacier
current.descent: From the summit/north ridge, descend the South Route, class 3-4 scrambling with some rappels and snow traversal to the Spider-Formidable col (crossover saddle), then follow the Ptarmigan Traverse route back across the Middle Cascade Glacier and Red Ledge to the Kool-Aid Lake camp.
current.detailed_rack: A 60m or 70m rope, a single set of cams from about 0.3-3 in (e.g. BD Camelots), a set of nuts, a few small Mastercams, and 2 pickets.
current.pro_needs: A single light rack (cams 0.3-3in, nuts, a few small Mastercams) covers the 5.6 rock; 2 pickets and an ice axe/crampons cover the couloir and glacier; an anchored belay is recommended for crossing the moat at the top of the glacier.
bivy: Cache Col and the Cache Glacier shoulder
current.rope_note: Published rack from a documented second ascent trip report: crampons, 60 or 70m rope, ice axe, single set BD Camalots 0.3-3in, set of nuts, some small Mastercams, helmet, and 2 pickets. 8-12 pitches of glacier travel plus moderate rock to 5.6.

name: Northeast Ridge (1963 Route)
beta: Grade: 5.7+ YDS, Grade IV, 12 pitches, 4,000 feet. First ascent: 1963. Route: Climb partway up C-J couloir to hanging glacier on right; ascend leftmost rib to summit. Hazards: Objective danger from falling rock/ice, steep snow, exposed scrambling, avalanche potential. Equipment: Small-to-medium alpine rock rack (to 3 inches), 10+ runners, helmet. Best season: July-September. No bush climbing.
overview: A more direct, all-rock alternative to the neighboring East Ridge and Northeast Buttress lines: climbs partway up the Cascade-Johannesburg Couloir to a hanging glacier, then follows the leftmost rib to the summit, deliberately avoiding the brush that plagues the other routes.

current.approach: East/Northeast from Cascade Pass trailhead; descend and cross Cascade River, then approach the northeast face via C-J couloir
approach_variant_names: Straight off the road end: the C-J couloir to the hanging glacier, then the leftmost rib
current.descent: From the summit, follow the East Ridge — downclimbing/rappelling loose, exposed 3rd/4th-class gendarme ledges (staying well below the crest) — to the Cascade-Johannesburg col. From the col, either rappel the C-J couloir or take the "Doug's Direct" line: traverse beneath the Triplets buttress, sidehill steep heather/meadow slopes, cross the north ridge of Mixup Peak, and descend to Cache Glacier, then follow the Cascade Pass trail back to the trailhead. This descent has taken other parties on Johannesburg's NE-aspect routes on the order of 4.5-9+ hours from the col.
current.detailed_rack: A small-to-medium alpine rock rack up to about 3 inches and 10+ runners/slings.
current.pro_needs: Standard alpine rock rack to 3 inches with plenty of runners for the 12-pitch rib; supplement with snow/ice protection for the lower couloir approach.
current.rope_note: 12-pitch Grade IV 5.7+ alpine ridge with steep snow/mixed approach terrain. Ice axe/crampons often needed for approach snow depending on season.

name: Northwest Face
beta: A squeeze chimney and friction slab low on the route lead to a well-protected layback/jam crack for the standout second pitch, followed by flared corner-crack systems and a final stemming open-book/gully pitch to third-class terrain just below the summit. Several sections are rated R for sparse protection, so this is a more serious Grade II than the rating alone suggests.
overview: A five-pitch, 500-ft line of cracks, chimneys, and a friction slab up Kangaroo Temple's Northwest Face, combining sustained 5.7 climbing with notably sparse protection in places.

current.approach: The Temple (Kangaroo Temple, on Kangaroo Ridge) is reached from the large pullout at the hairpin turns on SR-20 just east of Washington Pass — the same parking area used for the neighboring Hairpin Crags/Spire Gully climbs. From the pullout, a climber's trail heads south across a boulder field, through forest and more talus (faint, intermittently cairned) up to Kangaroo Pass, about 1 hour. From the pass, an intermittent trail traverses to a gully between Kangaroo Temple and Little Finger; ascending or descending that gully reaches the base of the North Face, Northwest Face, or Southwest Face routes, roughly another hour. Expect about 11 hours car to car. For this specific route: boulder field to Kangaroo Pass, traverse left to the gully between Kangaroo Temple and Little Finger, then ascend toward the notch. Northwest Face breaks off onto a climber's trail about 200 ft below the notch instead of continuing into the boulder-choked gully.
approach_variant_names: The Hairpin turnout and Kangaroo Pass, then break off the gully about 200 ft below the notch
current.descent: From the summit, downclimb or scramble to the fixed rappel anchors on the north side of the formation. Accounts differ slightly — some parties do two full-length 30 m rappels, others do three shorter single-rope rappels (roughly 150-160+ ft total) to avoid rope-stuck issues — landing at or near the North Ridge notch. From the notch, continue the standard descent gully back down to Kangaroo Pass and retrace the approach trail to the trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: Single rack of cams roughly 0.3-3" (some parties double up 0.4-1") plus a full set of nuts; carry a #4/#5-size chock or large cam for the sparsely protected squeeze chimney on pitch 1.
rack: 8 alpine draws (extra-long slings recommended for the wandering pitches)
Single 60m rope (or two 30m ropes for the alternate scramble-off descent)
current.pro_needs: Single rack to 2" plus a set of nuts/chocks is the baseline; a #3 and #3.5 cam can supplement but aren't strictly required. Protection is genuinely sparse/runout in sections (R-rated by multiple trip reports), so solid placement judgment matters more than gear volume.
bivy: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
current.rope_note: 5-pitch 5.7+ face route (first ascent Beckey brothers, 1942); pitches wander so extra long slings recommended. Descent: two 30m raps to a scramble-off ledge, or three raps to the notch with a 60m rope.

name: Northwest Face (Boving-Pollock)
beta: P1 is a committing traverse and corner (~10 hard moves) to a ledge belay; P2 is a right-facing corner with limited feet and hard gear placement (5.11a); P3 is a chimney then vegetated crack over a block (~5.8); P4 is a scramble approach to the overhangs; P5 pulls a pair of obvious overhangs with good protection (~5.10); P6 finishes with hand-crack climbing to the summit (~5.9).
overview: A varied alpine free climb up the west face of South Early Winter Spire, beginning low on the northwest face and traversing into the famous double-roof 'Boving Roofs' pitch before finishing up the Southwest Rib. First ascended (aid) by Boving & Pollock in 1976; freed by Boving & Kerns in 1977.

current.approach: From the Blue Lake Trailhead, follow the Blue Lake Trail about 1-1.25 miles (roughly an hour) to the clearing/meadow on the spire's northwest side. Leave the trail on the well-worn climber's path and ascend talus and heather into the basin directly below the northwest face — this is the same basin used to access the Southwest Rib, Mojo Rising, and Free Mojo, so route-finding to the base is shared. The Boving-Pollock start is identifiable by a steep corner system; the first pitch traverses into the corner and makes committing moves (~5.10ish) up to a prominent ledge, where some parties belay while others continue to a tree-anchored stance.
approach_variant_names: Blue Lake Trail to the northwest clearing, then the basin below the northwest face and the steep corner system
current.descent: The northwest face is the shorter of SEWS's west-side lines (6 pitches), and parties typically continue to the true summit and take the standard South Arete descent: downclimb the arete (3rd/4th class with a short 5th-class step) to the Rabbit Ears, then 3 single-rope rappels (60m rope) from bolted anchors/chains down the gully to the base, returning via the climber's trail to Blue Lake Trail. There is no route-specific rappel-the-face option, so bailing mid-route would mean building natural gear anchors (pitons/cams noted in the route description) rather than relying on fixed hardware.
current.detailed_rack: Standard rack with extra TCUs or aliens.
rack: Standard trad rack 0.3-3in cams, small-mid nut set
Extra small cams (TCUs/Aliens) for pitches 1-2 (sparse gear)
Single 60m rope; the descent rappels are all single-rope
current.pro_needs: Committing moves above gear on P1 and P2; extra small cams recommended.
current.rope_note: 6-pitch 5.11a Boving-Pollock line on SEWS's NW face; the South Arete descent is three single-rope rappels on a 60m rope.

name: Standard Route / Northwest Spire
beta: From the Redoubt Glacier saddle (high camp at 7,150 ft), traverse to the northeast ridge saddle below the col between the twin spires. Climb 2-3 pitches of Class 4-5 rock (crux involves manteling wet slabs) to gain the ridge crest. Continue with Class 3-4 ridge scrambling and occasional low 5th class moves to the summit. Lichen and water seepage make holds unreliable; test all holds before committing weight.
overview: Northwest Mox Peak ('Easy Mox') is the lower of the Twin Spires (Mox Peaks), a remote and technical summit deep in the Chilliwack Range about four miles south of the Canadian border. Its standard route climbs class 4 to low-5th-class rock (roughly 5.5) in a committing, seldom-visited position, typically approached by crossing into Canada and back.

current.approach: Drive 31.7 miles on Chilliwack River Road from Chilliwack, BC, then turn left onto narrow Depot Creek Road (high-clearance 4WD recommended for the upper 2.5 miles). Park at 2,350 ft where the road becomes impassable. Follow old logging road 2 miles to the Washington state border and official trail start. The trail climbs steeply in the final 0.5 miles through forest to Depot Creek Falls. Scramble up a climber's trail past the waterfall (fixed ropes assist) to reach Ouzel Lake (5,700 ft) in roughly 6-9 hours with 3,500 ft elevation gain. From Ouzel Lake, scramble up the steep Class 3 buttress southwest of the lake to access Redoubt Glacier. Ascend the glacier approximately 2 miles, traversing WSW and climbing to a flat area around 7,300 ft, then contour southeast to the saddle below the col between the spires at approximately 7,200 ft (3.2 hours, 1,550 ft gain from lake). Total approach: roughly 9-12 hours from trailhead to high camp.
approach_variant_names: Depot Creek, Lake Ouzel and the Redoubt Glacier traverse
current.descent: Downclimb/reverse the ridge to the headwall, then rappel: parties commonly make several rappels down to the ridge's low point followed by a long double-rope rappel back onto Redoubt Glacier, then reverse the approach to camp.
current.detailed_rack: Single set of small-to-mid cams (~0.3-2 in), several nuts, 4-6 slings/draws, two ropes — the rappels off the summit tower are single-rope, but the last one, from the ridge saddle back onto the Redoubt Glacier, is a full ~60 m double-rope rappel that a single rope will not reach; separate glacier travel kit (prusiks, pulley, pickets as conditions warrant).
current.pro_needs: Exposed alpine rock to roughly 5.5; a standard rack and rope handle the crux and the rappel descent.
bivy: Ouzel Lake basin, head of Depot Creek

name: Northwest Ridge
beta: After a long approach across the Inspiration and McAllister Glaciers, the Northwest Ridge offers three short (each well under 25 m/rope-length), moderate pitches to the summit — the easiest established route on the peak, popular as a descent for other routes.
overview: The Northwest Ridge is Dorado Needle's easiest and most-traveled technical route: a striking arete high above the McAllister Glacier with sweeping views, first climbed in July 1940 by Lloyd Anderson, Karl Boyer, and Tom Gorton — the peak's first ascent. It's a moderate glacier approach followed by 2-3 short, clean pitches (5.4) to the summit.

current.approach: Reach the base via the shared Eldorado Peak approach: from the large trailhead parking area on Cascade River Road (~2,100 ft, about 20 miles from Marblemount), backtrack a short distance downstream to find a log or ford crossing of the Cascade River, then pick up the climbers' path heading east/upstream on the far bank. The unmaintained boot path climbs through forest and then talus (roughly 1,500 ft of gain) before breaking into open slopes; stay right of the large windfall area and avoid crossing Eldorado Creek. Cairns and flagging lead up and right into a broad basin around 5,500-5,800 ft (Roush Creek/Eldorado Basin), where scattered camps exist near 6,100 ft; most parties push on to an Inspiration Glacier high camp near 7,400-7,600 ft (roughly 5.3 mi and ~5,300 ft gain, 5-6 hours car-to-camp). From high camp, rope up and cross the Inspiration Glacier, pass through/near the Tepeh Towers, and drop onto the McAllister Glacier, favoring its left (south) side to dodge a large crevasse that opens on the right later in the season. Ascend the McAllister's steep upper apron (~30°) trending northwest to its top, below a line of gendarmes on Dorado Needle's northwest ridge crest. Watch for a moat where the glacier meets the rock — find a safe crossing point, which can deteriorate significantly by late summer — then climb a short low-5th-class pitch to gain the ridge. Crevasse hazard on both glaciers and a moat at the base are the main approach-specific concerns; carry pickets for the snow.
approach_variant_names: Inspiration to McAllister, then the small col at the toe of the ridge
current.descent: Descend by downclimbing or rappelling the same Northwest Ridge line used on ascent. A single rappel down the final snow/rock step back to the glacier is typical, though parties sometimes downclimb this section instead if conditions allow; a 30m rope suffices for the short rock pitches, but bring a 60m single if you intend to rappel the snow pitch in one go rather than making two shorter raps. Anchors are a mix of old fixed tat on rock horns and slung natural features (horns/chockstones) rather than bolts — carry a handful of extra double-length slings and a few feet of cord/webbing to back up or replace worn anchor material, and inspect any in-situ tat carefully (one party reported an anchor block dislodging during a rappel here). The rock is fractured with loose flakes prone to catching or dislodging the rope, so manage rope stacking and pull carefully. Below the rappel, re-cross the moat (which can worsen through the season) back onto the McAllister Glacier, then reverse the approach across the McAllister and Inspiration Glaciers to high camp. An alternate snow-gully descent line exists off the ridge but is guarded by a large moat that typically still requires a short rappel to bypass, so it offers little advantage over the standard ridge descent.
current.detailed_rack: Small rack to 2.5 inches (cams and nuts), and about 6 ft of extra webbing for the rappel anchor.
current.pro_needs: Light rack — small-to-mid cams and nuts suffice for the short ridge pitches; slings for horn anchors.
bivy: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road

name: Northwest Ridge
beta: This ridge was first climbed in 2018 as one leg of the 'Boston Marathon' — a ~26.2-mile, mostly-soloed technical traverse circling the entire rim of Boston Basin (26 pitches up to 5.8 R, 26 rappels, 20,000+ ft of technical terrain). The ridge itself is deep, virgin choss rated 5.5 X, including a two-pitch section climbed à cheval (straddling the ridge crest) across rock with the consistency of feta cheese, followed by roughly 1,000 additional feet of similarly poor climbing. It is accessed along the basin rim from the direction of Sharkfin Tower. There is no established description of this specific ridge as an independent route — treat it as an obscure, rarely-repeated line rather than a maintained trade route.
overview: Boston Peak's northwest ridge is an obscure, seriously run-out line linking the Sharkfin-Boston col to Boston's summit. Its only known ascent came in July 2018 as part of the 'Boston Marathon,' a west-to-east enchainment that circled Boston Basin over Forbidden Peak, Sharkfin Tower, Boston Peak, and beyond (VI 5.8 R overall). The ridge itself is deep, virgin choss — rock the consistency of feta cheese — including a two-pitch à cheval traverse and roughly 1,000 more feet of climbing rated 5.5 X, much of it climbed unroped. No other ascents are known; treat this as an unrepeated, essentially unprotectable objective for very experienced parties rather than an established route.

current.approach: There is no standalone approach described for this ridge. What is confirmed is that the ridge connecting Boston Peak toward Forbidden Peak passes over Sharkfin Tower (8,120+ ft), and the only known ascent reached it via a multi-day connecting traverse begun on Forbidden Peak rather than as a direct approach to Boston. For a party attempting it directly, the most logical line mirrors the standard access used for the Forbidden/Torment/Sharkfin ridge system: from the Cascade River Road pullout just past mile marker 22 (across from Johannesburg Mountain), follow the old mining road about 0.75 mile to the historic mine site, then the steep, eroded Boston Basin climbers' path — with four stream crossings — up through forest to treeline near 5,300 ft. Boston Basin proper sits at ~5,700 ft, with a low camp around 5,300 ft and a high camp around 6,400 ft. From high camp, glacier travel up the Quien Sabe/Boston Glacier basin toward the col between Sharkfin Tower and Boston would put a party at the low (northwest) end of this ridge; from there the crest itself has no published route description, so expect sustained, likely-loose 4th-class-or-harder ridge climbing with route-finding as the real crux. The line from high camp to the col is the logical way in, not an established approach for this ridge.
current.descent: No descent-only beta exists for this ridge — the first-ascent party continued their traverse onward (over to Sahale Peak and down Sahale Arm) rather than retreating back down it, so going down this way is undescribed. A party that climbed the ridge and topped out on Boston's summit would most sensibly descend via the Southeast Face route's established rappel line (3 rappels down the southeast/east face on fixed slings to the Boston Glacier — see that route) rather than reversing the ridge, since that is the only descent off this peak with known, documented anchors. Retreating directly back down the Northwest Ridge itself should be assumed to mean natural, self-built anchors the whole way (slung horns/chockstones or gear placements) with zero documented stations and the same loose rock the route is known for — a serious, committing proposition that should not be planned around finding fixed gear.
current.detailed_rack: A light alpine rock rack weighted toward small-to-mid cams (roughly 0.3-2in) and a modest nut set — the first-ascent party found the rock as crumbly as feta cheese and the crux to be two pitches of a-cheval straddling a crumbling ridge crest, meaning placements will be scarce and often marginal rather than plentiful. This is not a route to bring a full double rack for; prioritize a few bomber pieces you can trust over volume. Given the X rating (runout/poor pro), extra cordage/slings for improvised anchors off horns, chockstones, or rock features is worth the weight, since natural gear placements can't be counted on.
current.pro_needs: Protection is genuinely sparse — this is an X-rated route, meaning real runout on rock described firsthand as extremely rotten ('virgin choss'). The only detailed account treats significant sections as essentially unprotected and relies on careful movement (a-cheval technique) rather than gear over a crumbling crest. Don't expect reliable natural anchors; back up placements
bivy: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins

name: NW Face Var. (Remsberg Variation)
beta: Shares P1 and P2 with the standard Northwest Face. On P3, rather than the 5.8+ flakes pitch to the right, climb a well-protected crack trending slightly left (5.7) for ~40 ft, place a final solid 1-2" piece where the crack narrows, then continue up a 5.10 flared groove past two bolts and tricky slab to the belay ledge. P4-5 rejoin the standard Northwest Face to the west summit.
overview: A harder finish variation to the standard Northwest Face route, established by Dale Remsberg and Scott Stimpson. Replaces the standard route's third pitch with a direct crack and a flared 5.10d groove past two bolts, then rejoins the standard line for the last two pitches.

current.approach: Identical to the standard Northwest Face route, since this is a single-pitch variation on it: from the Blue Lake Trailhead, hike the Blue Lake Trail ~1.5 miles to the meadow, take the climbers' path left past the small stream, and follow it toward Concord as far as it goes before breaking left onto the short low-5th-class step that gains Liberty Bell's NW plateau. The Remsberg Variation only diverges from the parent route at the 3rd pitch belay — everything below that is the standard NW Face approach.
approach_variant_names: Blue Lake Trail, the gully split, and the west-side bench
current.descent: The variation rejoins the standard NW Face route above pitch 3 (it climbs a more direct crack to the same belay ledge the original pitch 3 reaches), so pitches 4-5 and the descent are identical to the Northwest Face: from the west summit, scramble to the top of the Beckey Route and use its rappel line. From the summit, downclimb the upper pitch a short way and go left (east) to a tree hung with rappel slings. One single-rope rappel with a 60 m rope reaches a sandy ledge; work right and down to a bolted station, then make two single-rope rappels of about 25 m from bolted anchors into the Liberty Bell-Concord notch at about 7,300 ft. Parties who downclimb the ridge and the 5.6 boulder problem to the first bolts instead of making the tree rappel do two rappels in all. From the notch, downclimb the loose gully back to the climbers’ path and the Blue Lake Trail.
current.detailed_rack: Gear to 2" covers the variation pitch; two bolts protect the upper flared-groove/slab section.
rack: Gear to 2in cams, standard nut set
6 alpine draws/quickdraws (final crux 40ft is bolt-protected, no gear placements)
current.pro_needs: Well protected to the point the crack narrows, then relies on 2 fixed bolts through the flared groove/slab finish.
current.rope_note: Standard 60m inferred for a 5-pitch Washington Pass alpine rock route.

name: NW Ridge
beta: The Northwest Ridge is the moderate line on Colchuck Balanced Rock and the route of choice for parties who want the summit rather than the west face's hard free climbing. The line gains an obvious gully from Colchuck Lake to the notch above Jabberwocky Tower, then third-class terrain leading to the ridge proper, followed by the sharp ridge at 5.6 to the summit. Total gain from the Stuart Lake Trailhead to the summit is about 4,760 ft, and a relaxed car-to-car time is roughly 12 hours. The final obstacle is the balanced summit block itself, a short boulder problem that most parties protect. Descent from the summit was a single 25 m rappel off an anchor down the east side, then scrambling talus around to the south saddle and back past Jabberwocky Tower to Colchuck Lake. The rock is granodiorite. The peak's first ascent was made in 1958 by Gene Prater and Thomas Quin, though not necessarily by this line.
overview: A moderate scramble/low-5th-class ridge route on the northwest side of the formation, approached from the east side of Colchuck Lake. Class 3 terrain leads to a notch above Jabberwocky Tower, followed by a few pitches of low 5th class up to 5.6 along the exposed ridge crest to the summit area.

current.approach: Hike the Stuart Lake Trail (#1599) and the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599.1) from the Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road) — 4 miles and 2,280 ft gain, crossing Mountaineer Creek on a log bridge at 1.5 miles and staying left at the Lake Stuart Trail junction — to reach Colchuck Lake (2.5-3 hours). Unlike the west-side routes, the NW Ridge is approached from the east side of the lake: work around the eastern shoreline/talus to the base of the obvious gully that splits toward the notch above Jabberwocky Tower, the granite spire between the lake and Colchuck Balanced Rock. Ascend this gully (loose in spots, rope-up terrain for the upper section) to the notch, then move onto class-3 ground on the NW Ridge proper before the climbing begins. One documented ascent clocked roughly 4,760 ft of total gain and a 12-hour car-to-car day, consistent with the route's ~18.5 km round-trip distance.
approach_variant_names: Colchuck Lake east shore to the Jabberwocky Tower notch
current.descent: From the ridge's high point (below the exposed summit boulder problem, which most parties do not attempt due to thin protection), descend via a single ~25m rappel down the east face off a fixed anchor — a natural sling/horn setup rather than bolts, so inspect it before committing. After the rappel, scramble down talus and broken rock slopes, contouring around to a saddle on the south side, back past Jabberwocky Tower, and down to Colchuck Lake to rejoin the standard hike-out. Loose rock and route-finding through the talus are the main descent hazards; this is not a walk in fading light without a headlamp given the boulder-hopping involved.
current.detailed_rack: A light alpine rack suffices for 5.6 ridge climbing on granodiorite: a single set of cams roughly from small to #2 Camalot, a set of nuts, a good number of long slings for the ridge's horns and blocks, and a 60 m rope, which also covers the 25 m descent rappel. Bring a cordelette and some spare tat for building or backing up belays and the rappel anchor.
rack: Light trad rack (small-to-medium cams and nuts)
Single 60 m rope (covers the ~25 m descent rappel)
current.pro_needs: Minimal and mostly slung. The sharp ridge takes long slings over horns and blocks more than it takes cam placements, so weight the rack toward runners. A single set of cams and nuts covers the occasional crack. The only place where protection genuinely matters is the summit block itself, which is a short but seriously exposed V1 boulder problem — most parties belay it rather than solo it.
bivy: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road
current.rope_note: Class 3 to gain the ridge, then exposed 5.6 ridge climbing to a summit boulder-problem block; one party describes a single 25m rappel off a sling anchor on descent (consistent with a 60m rope doubled).

name: West Side (LeConte Glacier)
beta: Old Guard is usually tagged as a side-trip from a Ptarmigan Traverse camp near the Le Conte-Sentinel col (roughly 7,300-7,400 ft). From the col, rope up and cross the Le Conte Glacier, skirting crevasses and a bergschrund, to reach a snow ramp on the peak's northwest side. Above the ramp the route eases into a straightforward but somewhat loose, indistinct class 2-3 rock scramble to the summit. Most parties climb neighboring Sentinel Peak from the same camp in the same outing.
overview: Old Guard Peak rises near Le Conte Mountain and Sentinel Peak along the southern half of the Ptarmigan Traverse, just south of Cache Col in Glacier Peak Wilderness, overlooking the Le Conte and South Cascade Glaciers. A precision differential-GPS survey puts it at 8,260 ft, a few feet above neighboring Sentinel Peak, and its prominence makes it a worthy detour for traverse parties.

current.approach: Drive Cascade River Road east from Marblemount roughly 23 miles (paved for about the first 10, then good gravel) to its end at the Cascade Pass Trailhead (3,660 ft; parking area and vault toilet, North Cascades NP wilderness permit required for overnight camps). In some seasons, including 2026, the road is gated to vehicles at Eldorado (mile 20), leaving the last 3 miles to the trailhead on foot or bike. From the trailhead, follow the Cascade Pass Trail, which switchbacks about 30 times up a forested rib, gaining roughly 1,400 ft in the first 2 miles before the grade eases into a long ascending traverse through meadows, talus, and lingering snowfields to Cascade Pass (5,400 ft) at about 3.7 miles — figure 2.5-3.5 hours to the pass. This is only the start: Old Guard Peak sits deep in the Ptarmigan Mountains and is normally reached via the classic Ptarmigan Traverse, not as a day trip from the pass. From Cascade Pass, leave the maintained trail and climb south and east on a boot path/talus toward Cache Col (~6,900 ft), a rocky saddle roughly 3 hours above the pass; a steep snowfield on the col's far side (often needing an axe and crampons through midsummer) descends to Kool-Aid Lake basin (~6,320-6,800 ft), a common first camp about 6-8 miles and 2,800 ft of gain from the trailhead. From Kool-Aid Lake the route crosses a band of steep snow (pickets useful) to reach the Red Ledge, an exposed but broad Class 3 rock traverse that is the traverse's first real crux, especially if snow-covered. Beyond the ledges, follow the true-left (climber's left) edge of the Middle Cascade Glacier, roping up for crevasse hazard, staying on the less-broken upper glacier, then continue to the Spider-Formidable Col (a whiteout-prone spot where altimeter/compass/GPS route-finding matters). From the col, descend steep snow and a long sidehill traverse over snow and rock down to Yang Yang Lakes, then continue via LeConte Pass and Sentinel Pass to White Rock Lakes/the LeConte Glacier area — the standard second or third camp, roughly 12-14 hours of cumulative travel from the trailhead for parties moving efficiently. Old Guard Peak is climbed from Sentinel Pass: contour onto the LeConte Glacier and ascend a moderate, gradually-angled snow couloir/snowfinger on the peak's northwest side (watch for a bergschrund/moat late season) to gain the summit ridge, then finish on short, low-Class-3 scrambling on solid, high-friction gabbro to the true summit (8,240-8,260 ft). Water is available at Kool-Aid Lake, Yang Yang Lakes, and White Rock Lakes/tarns near the LeConte Glacier; carry a full topo map and glacier gear, as this is committing, remote glacier terrain with no easy bail once past Cache Col.
approach_variant_names: Cascade Pass and the traverse corridor to the LeConte Glacier
current.descent: Reverse the line of ascent: the short rock scramble and the Class 2-3 snow couloir back down to the LeConte Glacier, then cross the glacier to the Le Conte-Sentinel col camp. In a high-snow year a couple of very short rappels off nuts or slings may be needed on the way down, so bring a few small pieces and cord. Watch the moat and bergschrund at the foot of the couloir, and rope up for the crevassed glacier on the return to camp.
current.detailed_rack: A rope per team and pickets or ice screws for glacier travel. No technical rock rack is used on this class 2-3 route.
current.pro_needs: None beyond glacier-travel protection - pickets/screws for crevasse rescue and a belay on the snow ramp if desired; the summit scramble itself is unroped class 2-3.

name: Northwest Ridge / PCT approach
beta: From the Snowgrass Flats trailhead, hike ~5.4 miles through forest and meadows to the PCT, then follow the PCT north/west around the mountain's flank to its high point. Leave the PCT on an unsigned boot path that switchbacks up scree/talus to the northwest ridge and follows it south to the summit; the last ~50 feet is loose Class 2–3 rock with real but manageable exposure. An alternate line gains the col between Old Snowy and Ives Peak and follows the ridge crest/just-south-of-crest to the top.
overview: Old Snowy Mountain sits on the Goat Rocks volcanic crest immediately next to the Pacific Crest Trail, at its highest point in Washington. It's one of the most accessible Goat Rocks summits precisely because the PCT does most of the elevation work: from Snowgrass Flats the trail climbs to an unsigned spur that leaves the PCT and switchbacks up scree and snow to a short, loose, mildly exposed Class 2-3 scramble at the top. The small McCall Glacier lies on the east face and a distinctive natural rock arch (~20 ft) stands near the summit. Old Snowy is frequently combined with a traverse to nearby Ives Peak.

current.approach: From the Snowgrass Flats Trailhead (end of FR-2150, elev. ~4,600 ft), start on Trail 96 (Snowgrass Flat Trail). When the Snowgrass Flats lot is full, park at Berry Patch Trailhead, about half a mile west along FR 2150 near Chambers Lake, where Trail 96 begins; it joins this route about 0.6 mile in, at the junction where the short hikers' path from the Snowgrass Flats lot comes in. The first stretch climbs gently through forest, crossing Goat Creek on a footbridge at about 1.9 miles. Around 2.4-2.6 miles in you'll hear and then reach the springs that form the head of Snowgrass Creek just off the trail to the right - the last reliable, easy water source before treeline. About 0.8 mile past that the trail fords Snowgrass Creek itself; there's no bridge, but logs and rocks usually allow a dry crossing except during heavy snowmelt, when it can run fast enough to require care. Just beyond the ford (~3.9-4 miles, ~5,800 ft) the trail breaks out of forest into the open heather meadows and wildflower bogs of Snowgrass Flat, a scenic rest and water-filter stop before the climb — note that camping is prohibited within Snowgrass Flat itself under Gifford Pinchot wilderness regulations (36 CFR 261.58(e)); parties camp instead at designated sites above/below the flats. Stay left on Trail 96 where the Bypass Trail 97 forks right toward Cispus Basin at about 3.9 miles, and continue straight past the Trail 86 junction (left, to Goat Lake) at about 4.7 miles, staying on the main track as it climbs in long benches with Mount Adams and the Goat Rocks opening up behind you. At about 5.4 miles the trail meets the Pacific Crest Trail at roughly 6,400 ft; turn left (north) onto the PCT. Follow the PCT north for about 1.8 miles, traversing rocky, increasingly exposed sidehill terrain on Old Snowy's west flank - snow patches can linger here into midsummer and may require an ice axe/traction for a secure traverse in early season. Watch for an unmarked climbers' path branching right (east) off the PCT toward a rocky saddle on Old Snowy's northwest ridge; take it and switchback steeply uphill for about a half mile. Many parties stash poles here for the final scramble: the last few hundred feet to the 7,880 ft summit are Class 2-3 hand-and-foot scrambling on loose rock, moderately exposed but not technical. Loose talus and rockfall kicked down by parties above are the main hazard on this final pitch, so avoid stacking directly below other climbers. Total one-way distance is approximately 7.5 miles with about 3,600 ft of gain; round trip is roughly 15.5 miles, typically taking 8.5-9.5 hours car to car. After leaving US-12 the approach road is about 16 miles of unpaved washboard; no big potholes in late August, but higher clearance is more comfortable.
approach_variant_names: Snowgrass Flat, the PCT north, and the unmarked climbers' path to the northwest ridge
current.descent: This is a walk-off, not a technical descent - there is no rappelling on the standard northwest ridge/PCT route. Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the Class 2-3 scramble off the summit block (the loose scree and blocky talus here is the descent crux - go slow, test holds, and stay alert for rock knocked loose by parties above or below you), then pick up the climbers' path back down to the PCT. From the PCT junction, follow the trail back south, again watching footing on any lingering snowfields on the exposed sidehill traverse below the ridge (these are firmest and safest to cross in the morning before they soften). Continue south on the PCT to the Trail 96 junction (~6,400 ft) and descend Trail 96 the way you came - back through Snowgrass Flat, across the Snowgrass Creek ford, past the spring/water source, and down through forest to the Snowgrass Flats Trailhead. No ropes, anchors, or rappel gear are needed for this route under normal summer conditions; a rope and basic glacier/snow travel gear are only warranted for early-season attempts with significant snow cover on the PCT traverse or summit scramble.
current.detailed_rack: No rack is needed — this is an unroped scramble.
current.pro_needs: No technical protection is used on the standard route — it is a trail hike to a Class 2–3 scramble finish. Trekking poles are commonly carried for the snowfields and loose talus.
current.rope_note: Class 2-3 non-technical scramble via the PCT and northwest ridge in the Goat Rocks; well-graded trail to a short loose/exposed final scramble. No rope needed under normal summer conditions.

name: Summit Block — North Face Direct Finish (variation)
beta: Approach the summit block from the north side (from Snow Dome and/or Crystal Pass traverse), then climb directly up the North Face instead of via the East Face ramps or northwest edge. This line is steeper and more exposed, with Class 5.4 climbing throughout.
overview: The most direct of the three summit-block finishes: a single ~80-ft pitch straight up the north face on mostly solid rock. It's the cleanest line on the pinnacle and conveniently shares ground with the north-side rappel descent.

current.approach: From the Hoh Rain Forest trailhead, follow the Hoh River Trail east through old-growth rainforest along the Hoh River.
