Established camps/toilets appear at roughly 5-Mile Island, the Olympus Guard Station (~9 mi, near the High Hoh Bridge), Lewis Meadow (~11 mi, 1,000 ft — the usual overnight on a 2-day approach, gravel bars/bear wire/privy), and Elk Lake (~15.5 mi) before the trail climbs steeply through forest to Glacier Meadows (17.3–17.4 mi, ~4,300 ft, community bear-wire, standard high camp). Watch for a washed-out, ladder-assisted cliffside stretch around mile 16 (rungs have been reported missing/broken in recent seasons), fallen-log stream crossings, and early-season steep snow on the lower trail calling for an axe; travel above Elk Lake carries avalanche exposure outside summer. Water is frequent the whole way. From Glacier Meadows a way-path climbs ~0.8 mi to the crest of the Blue Glacier's lateral moraine, then follows the moraine ~0.2 mi (steep, loose — some parties fix a short line) before dropping onto the ice; rope up here, crevasse-rescue kit mandatory. Cross the flat lower glacier and climb moderate snow, threading rock islands right of the main icefall before swinging back left below the massif, to Snow Dome (~6,600–6,800 ft), a common high camp ~1,000 ft below the summit. From Snow Dome most parties take the Crystal Pass line: up to and across Crystal Pass, then traverse just south of (below) Five Fingers Ridge, over a false summit, to the base of the true (West) summit block at ~7,900 ft on its northeast side, beneath the ~80 ft summit tower. A large crevasse near Crystal Pass is usually snow-bridged through midsummer but can open late season; the steepest snow (~40–45°) has a clean runout in normal conditions, and a developing moat at the rock's base in warm/late-season conditions can force a committing step onto the rock.
approach_variant_names: Hoh River Trail, Blue Glacier and Snow Dome to the base of the summit block
current.descent: The North Face Direct Finish climbs straight up the ~80 ft north face on generally solid rock (5.4, one pitch) rather than the standard east-face ramp system — enough parties end up on this exact line that a semi-permanent rap anchor has built up at the top: a boulder/horn rigged with slings, a rap ring, and a quick link (inspect and back up any fixed tat, it is not agency-maintained). The rappel is roughly 80 to 100 ft from the summit down to the snow at the block's base — which a 60 m rope doubled (30 m/strand) reaches with room to spare. Bring a full 60 m rope, or plan to link two 30 m ropes, or use the lower intermediate station some parties have rigged to split it into two shorter rappels if carrying a shorter (30–40 m) rope. This single double-rope rappel lands you back on the snow essentially at the base of this finish. From there, reverse Crystal Pass, Snow Dome, the Blue Glacier and lateral moraine, and the Hoh River Trail back to the trailhead, typically with another night at Lewis Meadow or Elk Lake.
current.detailed_rack: Rock rack of 8-10 cams, sizes 0.4-1.5 inches, quickdraws, and slings. The North Face is steeper and protection placements may be smaller and more sporadic.
current.pro_needs: Solid rock climbing ability and protection placement skills required. This is the most technical summit block variation.

name: Summit Block — Northwest Edge Finish (variation)
beta: After reaching the base of the summit block (via any approach), this variation climbs the northwestern edge of the block directly. The rock is generally more solid than the East Face, with several Class 5.3-5.4 moves. The exposure is significant but the climbing is more straightforward.
overview: A variation finishing up the solid northwest edge of the summit block, offering better rock quality than the East Face ramps but with more exposure.

current.approach: Same as Blue Glacier/East Face route approach until reaching the summit block base. Approach time is identical.
approach_variant_names: Hoh River Trail, Blue Glacier and Snow Dome to the base of the summit block
current.descent: Rappel from summit anchor down the northwest edge using a single rope to a belay ledge below, then downclimb and traverse to rejoin the standard descent route.
current.detailed_rack: Small rock rack of 6-10 cams, sizes 0.4-2.0 inches, with quickdraws and slings. The northwest edge offers more consistent protection placements than the East Face ramps.
current.pro_needs: Good protection placement and climbing technique required. This variation is more technical and exposed than the East Face ramps.
bivy: Glacier Meadows — the standard Blue Glacier base camp
Lewis Meadows Camp, Hoh River trail
Elk Lake Camp, Hoh River trail
Snow Dome / Caltech Rocks high bivy, on the Blue Glacier

name: Mount Olympus Traverse (West–Middle–East Peaks)
beta: After summiting the West Peak via the standard Blue Glacier route or a variation, descend to the saddle between West and Middle Peaks (this descent is not technical but involves careful route-finding and downclimbing). Cross to Middle Peak (7,929 feet), which has Class 3-4 scrambling. Continue to East Peak (7,762 feet) with additional Class 3-4 scrambling and potential crevassed terrain. Reverse the approach from the East Peak to descend back to Glacier Meadows via an alternative glacier system or retrace the standard route.
overview: A more complete tour of the Olympus massif that links all three of its main summits in one outing. After climbing the West Peak you continue over the Middle and East peaks, then drop off the far side via Glacier Pass — a longer, more committing day than the standard climb but a far fuller experience of the mountain's summit crest.

current.approach: Same Hoh River Trail (17.4 mi) and Blue Glacier approach to Glacier Meadows as the standard route (5-Mile Island, Olympus Guard Station/High Hoh Bridge, Lewis Meadow ~11 mi as the common overnight, Elk Lake, Glacier Meadows at 4,300 ft), then the ~1-mi lateral-moraine crossing onto the glacier. From Snow Dome (~6,600–6,800 ft), the traverse follows the standard Crystal Pass line — over Crystal Pass, south of (below) Five Fingers Ridge, over the false summit — to the West Peak (7,980 ft), then continues east across intervening terrain to the Middle Peak (7,929 ft) and finally the East Peak (7,762 ft). This is a multi-day, largely off-trail glacier and ridge outing; expect sustained glacier travel with crevasse and icefall exposure the entire way, and carry a full rescue kit for the whole traverse, not just the West Peak summit pitch.
approach_variant_names: Hoh River Trail, Blue Glacier and Snow Dome — the traverse begins on the West Peak
current.descent: Descending the West Peak summit block uses the same rappel as the standard route — a boulder/sling/rap-ring anchor giving a rappel of roughly 80 to 100 ft, comfortably inside a 60 m rope doubled. Continuing the traverse toward the Middle Peak, conditions matter a lot: the snow moat on the Middle Peak's east side is reported to run very deep in some seasons, and if it's not passable, parties have had to exit via Glacier Pass instead, which carries its own icefall hazard (the traverse line has to work around a heavily crevassed/icefall section on the upper Blue Glacier, staying right of the icefall before swinging back left below the massif). Some traverse parties also report a short rappel or careful downclimb off the Middle Peak's loose upper rock depending on the moat's condition that season — treat this as conditions-dependent rather than fixed. After the East Peak, the standard exit descends toward Glacier Pass and back down to Glacier Meadows, then reverses the Blue Glacier/moraine and the full Hoh River Trail to the trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: A light rack for the West Peak summit block: a few nuts or three or four small-to-medium cams, plus 3-4 slings for anchors. Most of the scrambling between summits is done unroped.
rack: Glacier travel kit: rope, crevasse-rescue gear
current.pro_needs: Self-reliance and route-finding ability are critical. Parties should be proficient in crevasse rescue and comfortable with unroped scrambling on exposed terrain.
bivy: Glacier Meadows — the standard Blue Glacier base camp
Snow Dome / Caltech Rocks high bivy, on the Blue Glacier
Lewis Meadows Camp, Hoh River trail
Elk Lake Camp, Hoh River trail
current.rope_note: Full glacier team-rope travel across the Blue Glacier/upper mountain (17+ mile approach, crevasses and bergschrunds) connecting West (7,980ft), Middle (7,929ft), and East (7,762ft) Peaks. West Peak's summit pitch needs 3-4 small-to-medium cams; Middle/East Peak sections are comparatively easier but still glaciated and exposed.

name: On the Prowl (D)
beta: Begins on blocky terrain at the downhill (toward-the-hairpin) end of the wall. Above the scrambly start the rock looks deceptively low-angle; scramble the lower section and trend right as it steepens, aiming for the arete after a short, exposed rightward traverse. Continue up varied knobs, crimps, and jugs. Near the top, traverse left on bolts through steeper, similarly-featured climbing to the anchors — the position and quality of climbing are better than the route looks from the ground, though the bolts themselves can be hard to spot before starting.
overview: A quirky single pitch beginning on blocky, scrambly ground at the downhill end of the Ice Box, climbing deceptively low-angle dark rock past an exposed traverse to an arete, then a bolted leftward traverse near the top to an anchor shared with a neighboring unnamed trad line.

current.approach: Park at the hairpin switchback on SR-20 between the Washington Pass summit and Early Winters/Mazama. Follow the climbers' trail up toward the chasm/gully right of the drainage, cross left below a slab, then scramble 3rd-class terrain up the left margin of the slabs into the Ice Box — about 15 minutes from the car. This route starts at the downhill (right-hand, toward-the-hairpin) end of the wall.
current.descent: Single pitch (21 m/70 ft) — lower directly from the top bolted anchor (fitted with rap hooks) back to the base; no walk-off needed.
current.detailed_rack: 7+ quickdraws for the bolts, plus the bolted top anchor (shared with the neighboring unnamed trad line at this crag); a 60 m rope is ample for this 21 m/70 ft pitch.
current.pro_needs: Bolt-protected (~7 bolts) with a bolted, hook-equipped anchor; no natural gear needed.

name: Open Book
beta: Starts at two wide, left-leaning cracks about 50 ft right of the base of the Classic Route; climbs up and left toward the shared anchors (block with tat and rings) used by The Roof.
overview: An easy, low-angle alternative up wide left-leaning cracks to the right of the Classic Route's base, sharing summit anchors with The Roof.

current.approach: Identical trailhead-to-basin approach as the Classic Route and The Roof: from the Snow Lake Trailhead on Stevens Canyon Road, hike the maintained Snow Lake Trail ~1 mile (about 350 ft of up-and-down) to Snow Lake, the last water source. Continue past the lake on the fading tread over a wooded rise, then pick a line up and right into the talus/dirt gully on the peak's NW side; a climbers' path reappears on a heather bench near the gully's top and leads into the basin beneath the summit block. Ascend moraine along the edge of the small basin snowfield to the saddle (Unicorn Col) just west/southwest of the summit, then follow the use trail traversing below the cliffs on the south side of the peak to the base of the summit horn. The Open Book line starts at two wide, left-leaning cracks about 50 ft right of the Classic Route on the same south face, so from the base of the horn move climber's-right before starting the technical climbing; it's regarded as the easiest of the summit-block lines (Easy 5th class / 5.0), a step down from the Classic Route (5.4-5.6) and The Roof (5.6). Total approach is roughly 2.5-3 miles one-way with about 2,400 ft gain, mostly on climbers' path and talus once past Snow Lake.
approach_variant_names: Snow Lake and Unicorn Col to the rightmost line on the summit horn
current.descent: From the top of the Open Book, either downclimb the same easy corner (viable given the route's easier grade, but still exposed near the top) or rappel using the same anchor system as the other summit-block routes: a large rock horn on the south side of the summit block, roughly 40-50 ft above the notch/base. Avoid the old dead tree/snag — it's reported as no longer trustworthy. A 30m rope is commonly reported as sufficient for the single-rope rappel, but multiple parties have found 30m to be marginal or just short depending on which of the two rappel lines off the horn you use (one reaches the south notch, the other drops toward the basin/glacier side), so a 40m rope removes any doubt. After reaching the ground, reverse the approach across the scree traverse, down through the basin and gully, past Snow Lake, and out the Snow Lake Trail.
current.detailed_rack: Big cracks favor #3-#4 Camalot-size cams; not much else needed.
current.pro_needs: Light rack; a rope and a few runners for the natural anchor and belay/rappel are the main requirement — approach shoes are fine, rock shoes not required.
bivy: Tatoosh cross-country zone bivy, basins below Unicorn and The Castle
current.rope_note: Second named line on the south summit-block face, rated 5.0.

name: Southwest Slopes Scramble
beta: From a camp at Lake Doris (6,975 ft), leave the trail and head roughly northeast through open forest for about 0.6 mile, then climb the long southwest-facing talus slope, gaining about 1,400 ft to the southwest ridge/south face before finishing to the summit (8,587 ft). Terrain is Class 2 throughout: loose scree low down giving way to talus and boulders higher up. A faint climber's path along the southwest ridge is reported to be easier going than a direct line up the boulder-strewn south face. As a climb from the south the peak is a long, tedious talus slog, while more involved, chossy climbing exists on the unfrequented east and north sides, which are not part of this standard route.
overview: Osceola Peak (8,587 ft per USGS; also cited 8,583-8,584 ft) is a remote Pasayten Wilderness summit in the Okanogan Range — the range's 10th-highest peak and #48 on Washington's Bulger List of the state's 100 highest summits. It sits on the ridge system connecting to Mount Carru (about 1 mile east) and Mount Lago, and was first climbed in 1933 by Hermann Ulrichs and Richard Alt. The north face is steep and cliff-bound, but the south/southwest slopes are a long scree-and-talus field giving a straightforward, if tedious, Class 2-3 scramble. Because the peak sits deep in the Pasayten backcountry, the 10-13+ mile wilderness approach — not the climbing itself — is the real crux of the trip.

current.approach: Trailhead: Slate Pass (~6,900 ft), the end of the Harts Pass Road (FR-5400) just below Slate Peak lookout — this is a full backpack approach, not a day hike (~13 miles/1,400+ ft one-way to base camp, within the ~28-mile round trip). From Slate Pass, drop off the pass on the old trail/way-trail toward the Whistler Cutoff Trail; this initial descent can hold snow well into summer (some parties carry an ice axe for it). The Whistler Cutoff Trail is an easy, well-graded downhill cruise to the Middle Fork Pasayten River, which is crossed unbridged — typically only ankle-to-shin deep in normal summer flow, but ford with care during early-season snowmelt or after rain. From the ford, join the Robinson Creek / Eureka Creek Trail system and follow it roughly to the Fred's Lake cutoff around the 9-10 mile mark; trail tread is in generally good, brush-free condition to this point. At the Shellrock Trail junction the maintained tread ends — travel beyond here is on a rougher, sometimes brushy path with blowdown. Climb past Fred's Lake to 7,100-ft Rolo (Fred's) Pass, then descend/contour a short, sometimes cliff-banded slope (route-find carefully here) into the Lake Doris basin (6,975 ft), a good camp with reliable water and the standard base camp for Osceola. From camp, leave the trail and go cross-country roughly 0.6 mile northeast through open forest, then talus, gaining about 1,400 ft up Osceola's long southwest-facing scree/talus slope to either the southwest ridge or south face. The south face is a slow, tedious boulder/talus slog; a faint but real climbers' trail on the southwest ridge (roughly 48.828, -120.583) offers noticeably better footing and is preferred by parties who've found it. Final scrambling to the 8,584 ft summit is Class 2-3. Watch for wet, lichen-covered rock on the upper slope, which gets slick fast in any moisture. In mid-July the trail to Lake Doris is in good shape, with a ford of the Middle Fork Pasayten and some blowdowns on the Eureka Creek trail.
approach_variant_names: Slate Pass, the Middle Fork Pasayten, and Fred's Lake to Lake Doris
current.descent: Walk-off/downclimb — no rappelling on this route (rappels: 0). Descend the same southwest-ridge climbers' trail or south-face talus/scree line used on the ascent back down to Lake Doris camp (about 1,400 ft of descent, roughly an hour); the ridge line is preferred over the direct south-face boulder field for better footing, especially on wet rock. From Lake Doris, reverse the full approach: climb back over 7,100-ft Rolo/Fred's Pass (mind the cliff-banded section just above the lake), pass Fred's Lake, pick up the Eureka/Robinson Creek Trail and Whistler Cutoff Trail, re-ford the Middle Fork Pasayten River, and climb back up to Slate Pass — roughly 13 miles and a full day's hiking each way, so most parties treat this as a 2-3 day backpack rather than a car-to-car push. No technical gear is needed for the descent beyond normal scrambling caution on loose scree and any lingering snow near Slate Pass. Descend the southwest ridge to the saddle, then drop scree back to your packs; this is easier than reversing the boulder field.
current.detailed_rack: None — this is an unroped Class 2 talus/scree walk-up; no climbing rack is carried.
current.pro_needs: Unroped class 2-3 scramble; no technical gear normally required.
bivy: Doris Lake and Freds Lake basins
current.rope_note: Nontechnical talus/scree scramble via SW ridge/south face from Lake Doris camp; no rope used on standard route.

name: Southeast Route
beta: From the Otto-Himmel Col (reached via Stump Hollow trail from Goodell Creek trailhead), ascend the east ridge directly to the summit. Early season (June–July): route is primarily snow with Class II-III scrambling near summit; descent is straightforward on consolidated snow. Mid-season (July–August): snow transitions to exposed rock; negotiable as Class III with careful foot placement. Late season (August–September): loose, tricky 5th class scrambling through chossy rock and talus fields. Final approach to summit features a fresh rockfall zone approximately 30 feet below summit ridge; experienced alpinists rope-protect the 5.7 pitches or navigate unstable terrain carefully. Route is approximately 500–700 vertical feet from col to summit.
overview: The Ottohorn is a slender granite spire in the Southern Pickets, rising directly across the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col from its larger neighbor Himmelgeisterhorn, deep in North Cascades National Park's Crescent Creek Basin. It was first climbed on September 10, 1961 by Ed Cooper, Glen Denny, Joan Firey, Joe Firey, and George Whitmore via the east ridge from the col (Class III) — the same trip that put up Himmelgeisterhorn and Frenzel Spitz, all three reportedly named after labels the Fireys peeled off a mustard bottle carried on the approach. One of the range's more obscure summits, Ottohorn is rarely climbed alone; most parties tag it as part of a Crescent Creek Basin enchainment with Himmelgeisterhorn and/or Frenzel Spitz.

current.approach: From the Goodell Creek trailhead (~600 ft, reached via the gravel road that forks off Hwy 20 across from Newhalem and dead-ends at a gravel pit — there's parking but no trailhead sign), follow the old abandoned logging roadbed paralleling the true-left/east bank of Goodell Creek. The first ~1.5 miles thread through dozens of downed trees and washouts on the roadbed before a real, if faint, trail emerges in the timber above; tread then levels out around 1,100 ft for roughly a mile. Around mile 3.5 (~1,700 ft) the trail crosses a stream — the last easy, reliable water for a long stretch — near a small campsite and a cairn marking the unsigned climbers' path up 'The Barrier,' the forested spur ridge that separates the Goodell/Terror Creek drainage from Crescent Creek Basin; fill bottles here. From the cairn the path steepens hard: a traverse around 3,200 ft, a talus field near 4,000 ft, a rock band around 4,800 ft, then a steep, brush-choked gully (early-season snow/ice up to ~35°) to a rocky streambed near 5,200 ft. Above that, heather benches and slabs lead to the crest of The Barrier, a ~6,200 ft notch that is the high point of the approach and the site of a common bivy. From the notch, descend ~250 ft into 'Stump Hollow,' the gentle basin between The Barrier and the Chopping Block, then contour on a long, rising traverse across the snow, slabs, and talus of Crescent Creek Basin — holding roughly the 5,800 ft level — to a camp near Mount Terror/Himmelhorn (around 7-9 miles and 6,000-6,500 ft of gain from the trailhead, consistent with this route's ~28 km round-trip distance). From camp, continue the rising traverse of Crescent Creek Basin toward the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col; crampon up the final snow/scree pitch to the col itself, which turns to loose, chossy class 3-4 scrambling once melted out late-season, with an overhanging boulder near the top sometimes forcing a chossy class 3/4 bypass on the left. A North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for the Crescent Creek Basin zone is required. Both The Barrier crossing and the basin traverse involve real route-finding on an unsigned, easily-lost climbers' path through heather and talus, and creek crossings near the trailhead can run high and fast on hot, high-snowmelt afternoons.
approach_variant_names: Goodell Creek, the Barrier notch and Stump Hollow, then the Crescent Creek Basin traverse to the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col
current.descent: Descend the Southeast Route by reversing the east ridge back down to the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col — a few pitches of low-5th-class downclimbing/scrambling to the notch. From the col, the standard return for this route is down the south side, back into Crescent Creek Basin: this is the easier, non-technical line (snow early season, loose class 3-4 talus/scree scrambling once late-season melt strips the snow) and does not require rappelling under normal conditions. If coverage is thin and a section of the loose downclimb feels too exposed, some parties back it off with a single short rappel off a sling on a natural anchor (block/horn) rather than downclimb it, but this is not the norm. Note that the north side of the col is a different, and harder, proposition and is not part of this route's own descent — parties continuing a traverse toward Himmelhorn/Mustard Glacier descend that side via one single-rope rappel from an established rap station about 150 ft below the col onto the Mustard Glacier (or, when well filled-in, a steep snow couloir); don't confuse that crossing with the Southeast Route's own walk-off. From Crescent Creek Basin, reverse the approach: traverse back to the base of The Barrier, regain the ~250 ft to the 6,200 ft notch, then descend the steep gully/talus/heather line back down to the Goodell Creek trail and out to the trailhead. Watch for loose rock in the gully below the Barrier notch and for creek crossings running high on hot afternoons. To continue on to Frenzel Spitz, descend roughly 500 ft from Ottohorn's north side, per the original 1961 first-ascent account.
current.detailed_rack: Bring a light rack of passive protection (nuts, hexes) and a few cams (size 00–2) for securing belays or protecting the 5.7 pitches used to bypass rockfall zones. Slings and cordage for creating anchors in scree and rock. Screwgate carabiners for safety. Most of the route is Class III solo scramble; the 5.7 option is backup for significant weather delays or if rockfall zone is extremely active.
rack: Light alpine rack: nuts/hexes and a few small cams (size 00-2)
Slings and cordage for anchors in scree/rock
current.pro_needs: A light alpine rock rack is sufficient for the scattered low-5th-class to 5.7 moves; belays are typically natural gear anchors rather than fixed stations.
bivy: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
High bivouacs at the western end of the crest
current.rope_note: Grade III-IV alpine rock in the Southern Pickets area; approach crosses glaciated terrain near Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col requiring rope for glacier travel.

name: Standard Scramble
beta: There is no single defined 'route' up Oval Peak so much as a set of interchangeable Class 2 ridge/slope lines that all converge near the summit. Parties commonly approach via the West Fork Buttermilk Trail No. 411 or the Oval Creek Trail No. 410A/Eagle Creek Trail, leave the trail in the basin below the peak, and climb whichever ridge (east, southwest, or south) looks cleanest that day, often descending a different one for better scree/talus conditions. The peak is defined by talus — talus, talus, and more talus — with large boulders higher up. A popular variation links Oval with neighboring Star and Courtney Peaks via the Fish Creek Pass / West Buttermilk Ridge traverse.
overview: Oval Peak (8,800 ft) is the highest summit in the Sawtooth Range and in the Methow Mountains subrange of the North Cascades, and the high point of the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness on the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest. It rises between Lake Chelan and the Methow Valley, with roughly 2,730 ft of prominence and about 15.5 miles of isolation, making it one of the more prominent yet lightly-visited summits in the range. The peak is notorious among Washington scramblers for its talus — nicknamed the ruler of a talus-choked 'Chossdom' — and the main challenge is route-finding among the many similar-looking gullies and ribs on the upper mountain rather than any single hard move. It's frequently combined with neighboring Star and Courtney Peaks on a multi-day Sawtooth Ridge traverse out of Buttermilk Creek, but also stands on its own as an overnight or long day trip from the Oval Creek drainage.

current.approach: Park at the Eagle Creek/Oval trailhead (~3,000 ft) at the end of FR 4420-080, reached via Twisp River Road/FR 44 (~12.5 mi west of Twisp) and the West Buttermilk/FR 4420 spur. From the trailhead, follow Eagle Creek Trail #410 for about 1.9 miles up the Eagle Creek valley (trail parallels the creek, so water is available) to the signed junction with Oval Creek Trail #410A. Bear onto #410A and climb steadily through forest along Oval Creek for roughly 7.5 more miles, passing West Oval Lake before reaching Middle Oval Lake (~6,700-6,800 ft) — about 9.5 miles and ~4,400 ft of gain from the car; there is good established camping near the lake's outflow if splitting the trip over two days. From the outflow, leave the maintained tread and scramble cross-country up open talus/scree slopes to the north/northeast to gain the Sawtooth crest at a broad saddle roughly 1,200-1,500 ft above the lake, then follow the rocky crest generally north/northwest over blocky, sometimes loose talus to Oval Peak's summit block. Much of this basin burned in the 2018 Crescent Mountain Fire, so the lower trail is exposed, dry, and dusty in summer with sections of soft/fragile burned ground that can give way underfoot — carry all the water you'll need once you leave Middle Oval Lake, since there are no reliable sources higher up. The crest scramble is class 2 but has real route-finding and loose-rock exposure in poor visibility.
approach_variant_names: Oval Creek trail to Middle Oval Lake
current.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: downclimb/scramble back along the Sawtooth crest talus to the saddle above Middle Oval Lake, then drop the scramble slope back down to the lake's outflow and rejoin the maintained Oval Creek Trail #410A. Retrace the ~7.5 miles down through the Oval Lakes basin (past West Oval Lake) to the junction with Eagle Creek Trail #410, and follow that 1.9 miles back to the trailhead. This is a class 2 talus/scree walk-down with no technical rappelling required in either direction — the main descent hazards are loose blocky talus on the crest (twisted-ankle/rockfall terrain, especially with other parties below) and the fragile burned tread lower on the trail. rappels: 0.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rock gear is used on the standard Class 2 route — it is a hike/scramble, not a roped climb.
current.pro_needs: Easy class 2 scramble; no technical gear normally required.
bivy: Oval Lakes basin - West and Middle Oval
current.rope_note: Class 2, unexposed boulder/talus ridge scramble via SW ridge from Oval Lakes or W Fork Buttermilk Creek; no rope needed.

name: East Face
beta: Approach via the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River trail to Dutch Miller Gap, then bushwhack to Overcoat Lake basecamp and contour to the Overcoat Glacier. Ascend the glacier, navigate crevasses and moats, then climb the exposed fourth class rock on the northeast side of the summit pyramid. Crampons and ice tools are essential. Descent is via downclimbing and rappels to return to the glacier.
overview: Overcoat Peak (7,432 ft) is the rugged, glacier-draped satellite summit immediately northwest of taller Chimney Rock, both crowning the ridge above the head of the Overcoat Glacier in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. It was named by USGS surveyor Albert H. Sylvester after he left his coat on the summit during a 1897 survey trip, an outing also considered the peak's first ascent. Overcoat sees far fewer visits than its taller neighbor because of the long, brushy approach up the Middle Fork Snoqualmie valley and the glacier travel required just to reach the base of the climbing. The true summit sits atop a steep roughly 400-foot rock block rising above the surrounding terrain on all sides, demanding sustained class 4 (occasionally low 5th-class) climbing no matter which side is used.

current.approach: From the Dingford Creek Trailhead (end of FR 56, Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road), the fastest approach uses the gated continuation of the road as a mountain-bike/hike-in: roughly 7-8 miles of old roadbed (NF-5620) to Hardscrabble Horse Camp near the old Dutch Miller Gap Trailhead, saving significant time over walking it. From there, follow the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River / Dutch Miller Gap Trail (Trail 1030) east along the north bank of the river for several more miles — the tread here is in reasonable shape with minimal blowdown, passing dispersed camps and, in season, overgrown thimbleberry brush that obscures footing on the lower tread. Roughly 13-14 miles in from the trailhead (about a mile before the trail crosses toward Williams Lake/Dutch Miller Gap proper), leave the trail and ford the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River — a real ford, potentially thigh-to-waist deep and cold with snowmelt, so time it for lower water and expect wet feet. On the far side, climb steep, brushy forest into the rocky defile some parties call the 'Valley of the Chiefs,' a roughly two-mile corridor that gains the bench below Overcoat Peak. Continuous snowfields typically begin around 4,600 ft; above about 6,600 ft the route alternates between rock and snow, with one sloping, exposed rock step that requires care to downclimb onto steep snow. A common camp is on rock slabs/benches around 6,600 ft directly overlooking the Overcoat Glacier, roughly 100 ft below the glacier's toe. Total trailhead-to-camp distance is on the order of 15-16 miles with 5,000+ ft of gain; this is a serious, mostly off-trail approach through wilderness terrain (Alpine Lakes Wilderness) with real route-finding, so a GPS track or careful map work for the Valley of the Chiefs and glacier-bench section is worthwhile. From camp, traverse west across the mellow lower-angle part of the Overcoat Glacier to reach the base of a snow finger on the peak's north/east side that leads to the summit rock.
approach_variant_names: Dingford Creek, bike the closed road, then ford the Middle Fork under the big cliff
current.descent: Reverse the ascent for most parties: from the summit, downclimb the Class 3-4 gully/ledge system on the peak's east side back toward the snow finger and glacier. Where the ledges pinch down at a dihedral feature (a damp, water-streaked corner reported by climbers), most parties do NOT free-downclimb the full corner — instead, build two rappels (roughly full 30m/60m-rope-length pitches) down the dihedral to regain the glacier below. Anchors are natural (slung horns, chockstones, or gear placements) rather than fixed bolts/chains — this is an alpine line with no fixed hardware, so carry a small rack and cordage for anchor-building and expect to leave gear (or plan to down-lead/simul on lower-angle sections to save equipment). A single 60m rope handles both rappels; parties without a 60m would need to break it into more, shorter rappels. Some parties instead find they can downclimb the full gully/ledge system without rappelling if conditions and confidence allow (reversing the ascent by downclimbing is the lower-commitment option), but the two-rappel dihedral descent is the more commonly reported method, especially when the rock is wet or holds are snow-covered. Below the glacier, retrace the approach: descend the Valley of the Chiefs (or, as at least one party has done, an alternate line down the main Overcoat drainage through open trees to avoid waterfall-forming cliffs lower down), re-ford the Middle Fork Snoqualmie, and rejoin the Dutch Miller Gap Trail back to Hardscrabble Horse Camp and the bike/hike-out to Dingford Creek Trailhead. Watch for loose rock in the gully/dihedral and for the river ford being higher/colder in the afternoon on hot days from glacier/snowmelt runoff.
current.detailed_rack: A few small-to-medium cams and nuts with slings for the summit pyramid; a 30m+ rope doubles as glacier rope (rope up for crevasse hazard) and rappel line if descending the east-side dihedral (two rope-length rappels reported).
current.pro_needs: Light rack (small-to-medium cams/nuts) for the class 4 summit pyramid, plus a standard glacier travel kit (axe, crampons, rope) for the Overcoat Glacier approach.
bivy: Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie

name: Painted Mountain Scramble
beta: From the North Fork Sauk trailhead, hike the maintained Red Mountain Trail (signed 'Painted Mountain Lookout Trail') about 1 mile to its end near the old 1936-67 lookout site (~2,800 ft). Ascend roughly 70 vertical feet of steep, moss-and-dirt-covered rock ledges (Class 3, exposed in spots) to gain the southwest ridge. From there a faint boot path, sometimes marked with pink flagging, climbs open meadows and rock along the ridge/shoulder to an overlook of Ruby Lake near 5,800 ft, then continues on steeper ground to about 6,700 ft before scree slopes lead to the 6,975 ft summit. The whole outing (car-to-car) is roughly 8 miles round trip with about 4,875 ft of total elevation gain.
overview: Painted Mountain (also historically called Red Mountain) is a distinctive red/orange, mineral-streaked 6,975 ft summit in the western Glacier Peak Wilderness, roughly 17-20 miles southeast of Darrington via the Mountain Loop Highway. Its Lushootseed name, 'Ska-hala-bats' ('painted'), was recorded by early Forest Service ranger Nels Bruseth; USGS surveyor Sam Strom had earlier dubbed it 'Red Mountain,' and 'Painted Mountain' became the official name in 1981 via the U.S. Board on Geographic Names. A fire lookout (1936-1967) once stood on a bench about a mile up the trail at roughly 2,800 ft, far below the summit, part of the dense North Cascades lookout network of the early-to-mid 1900s, and the peak was likely first climbed around 1897 by a USGS survey party. The mountain is built of Late Cretaceous migmatitic gneiss whose oxidized reddish-orange bands give it its name and its massive red-rock summit block.

current.approach: Park at the Sloan Creek Campground / North Fork Sauk trailhead (2,100 ft) at the end of FR 49. The signed trail here is the North Fork Sauk Trail #649, but the Painted Mountain route splits off almost immediately: look for the signed 'Red Mountain Trail' (a.k.a. Painted Mountain Lookout Trail) branching left about 100 yards in from the trailhead. Follow this boot path steadily uphill through forest for about 1 mile, gaining roughly 1,000 ft to where the maintained tread ends around 3,100 ft — this is the last reliable, easy-to-follow section. From 3,100 ft the route turns into a genuine scramble: climb a short but steep ~70-foot band of rock ledges covered in dirt and moss (roughly Class 3, the crux of the lower route — treat it as insecure, especially if wet) to gain the southwest ridge. Above the ledges the path thins to an intermittent boot track marked intermittently with old pink flagging; stay on the crest/southwest side of the ridge through open, flower-strewn meadows. Around 5,800 ft the visible path effectively disappears at an overlook above Ruby Lake — this is the key route-finding checkpoint; from here the line continues up steepening terrain (~300 ft of gain) staying on the right (west) side of the ridge crest. At about 6,700 ft you squeeze through a last band of stunted trees (again flagged with pink ribbon); above this there is no more ground cover, and the final several hundred feet to the 6,975-ft summit is loose scree and blocky rock. There is no reliable water past the trailhead/lower creek crossings, so carry what you need from the car; this is dry, south-facing, sun-exposed terrain in the upper half. Loose rock and scree-on-slab underfoot are the main hazards throughout the upper ridge, along with route-finding in fog since the flagging is sparse and the path is not maintained.
approach_variant_names: Sloan Creek Road, the lookout trail, and the southwest ridge
current.descent: This is a walk-off/downclimb — there is no rappelling on the standard route and no fixed anchors are known to exist on the peak. Descend by reversing the ascent line exactly: pick your way back down the loose scree and blocky rock below 6,700 ft, drop back through the flagged tree band, then follow the intermittent, pink-ribbon-marked boot path back down the southwest ridge past the Ruby Lake overlook (~5,800 ft) to the top of the Class 3 ledge band around 3,100 ft. Downclimb the ~70-foot dirt-and-moss ledge section facing in where it feels exposed (this is the spot most parties find harder in descent than ascent, and where loose rock underfoot is most consequential), then rejoin the maintained tread of the Red Mountain/Painted Mountain Lookout Trail for the easy 1-mile walk back to the North Fork Sauk trailhead. Total round trip is about 8 miles with roughly 4,875 ft of gain/loss, so budget a full day; the biggest descent hazards are loose talus/scree on the upper ridge and losing the faint path in poor visibility, not technical rope work.
current.detailed_rack: No rope or protection is used on the standard route; it is an off-trail Class 3 scramble.
current.pro_needs: None — no roped protection is placed on this route. Helmet for the loose ledge band; ice axe/crampons only if snow is present on the upper mountain.
bivy: Sloan Creek Campground and the North Fork Sauk road end
current.rope_note: Class 2-3 scramble to red-rock summit massif above ~3100ft; comfort with exposed scrambling needed but no rope typically used.

name: Painted Traverse
beta: From the summit of Painted Mountain, follow the crest east over broken ridge and snowfields to Magenta Peak. The section from Magenta to Black Mountain is the crux: the ridge is cut by numerous gendarmes that push you off the crest to find bypasses, with at least one awkward mossy downclimb. Black Mountain, the high point of the route, has several ways up: loose scree gullies on its southeast side; a steep heather chute from the basin on its south side to a small col just west of the summit block, then a short, exposed class 3 scramble up the northwest ridge; or, harder, a class 4 corner with slabby footholds on the north side. Descend Black's south side, over lingering snow early in the season, into the basin below it toward Brown Peak, whose summit can be skipped by crossing its shoulder. Continue south to the base of Skullcap Peak and tag it, then follow easier ridge with decent use paths over the Purple Peak area to Portal Peak. Drop to Red Pass on the Pacific Crest Trail and follow the crest to White Mountain, whose south ridge has a climber's path. Descend to White Pass.
overview: A long, colorful ridge traverse in the Glacier Peak Wilderness linking Painted Mountain, Magenta Peak, Black Mountain, Skullcap Peak, Portal Peak and White Mountain above the North Fork Sauk valley. Most of the line is heather, meadow and broken ridge, but gendarmes between Magenta and Black force committing route-finding and class 3-4 scrambling on loose rock. It is done as a loop from the North Fork Sauk trailhead, climbing steeply to Painted Mountain and returning from White Pass on the North Fork Sauk Trail.

current.approach: From the North Fork Sauk trailhead, the Red Mountain (Painted Mountain Lookout) Trail branches left about 100 yards in and climbs about a mile to the old lookout site near 3,100 ft. Beyond it an unmaintained climber's path goes straight up the slope with almost no switchbacks, including a short cliff band that needs class 3 scrambling, and continues steeply to the summit of Painted Mountain. Expect close to 5,000 ft of gain in under three miles.
current.descent: From White Mountain descend its south ridge to White Pass on the Pacific Crest Trail, then follow the North Fork Sauk Trail down switchbacks and through old-growth forest back to the trailhead. Parties that stop at Portal Peak can instead drop to Red Pass and take the same trail down.

name: Particulate Matter
beta: A thin crux comes in the first couple of bolts, with the third bolt set higher than ideal due to hollow rock near that stance. Above this, the climbing eases with slightly spaced bolts leading to the top of the wall.
overview: A moderate single-pitch sport route up the Ice Box right side wall, starting off a boulder in the creek bed right of an arching corner feature.

current.approach: From the large pullout at the SR-20 hairpin turn east of Washington Pass, follow the climbers' path uphill toward Spire Gully and the Quicksilver Slabs, then cut right into the dry creek bed below the chasm. Cross left beneath the first slab and scramble 3rd-class ground up the left edge of the smooth, slippery slabs into the Ice Box (a fixed line has been in place on the entry slab). Allow about 15 minutes from the car; expect snow on the approach early in the season.
current.descent: Single-pitch sport route; lower directly from the anchor at the top of the pitch back to the base. No walk-off or rappel needed.
current.detailed_rack: Fully bolted single pitch; roughly 10-12 quickdraws are enough to protect the 80 ft (24 m) route, plus a rope long enough to lower that distance.
current.pro_needs: Fully bolted sport climbing; no natural protection needed.

name: Standard Rock Route
beta: Pernod and neighboring Chablis are the easiest of the Wine Spires, and this line is a reasonable day from a Burgundy Col camp. The climbing is moderate (about 5.5-5.7) and not sustained. It climbs from the east side up to the notch between Pernod and Chianti and then up the northeast corner to a tiny summit block; the South Face and the Direct West Face are separate, harder routes on the same spire.
overview: Pernod is the highest of the four Wine Spires (Burgundy, Chianti, Chablis, and Pernod) above Washington Pass. Fred Beckey, Dick McGowan, and Don Wilde made the first ascent in September 1952, an aid-heavy climb by today's standards: pitons for both protection and direct aid, a hand-drilled Rawl-drive bolt to protect an insecure section, another bolt to facilitate an 8-foot pendulum around an overhanging, holdless corner, and more bolts placed from a shoulder-stand to reach the summit. The modern route follows essentially the same line, reached via the long Burgundy Col approach.

current.approach: From the roadside pullout on SR-20 about 0.7 mile past the Cutthroat Lake Road turnoff (directly across the highway from the Wine Spires), a boot/climbers' trail drops off the shoulder, crosses Early Winters Creek on logs or a rock-hop (can run high and require a wet ford in early-season snowmelt), and climbs a timbered rib on the climber's-left side of the Burgundy Creek drainage. The trail gains steeply and steadily — on the order of 2,000 ft over the first 1.5-2 miles — to a broad, flat bench at roughly 6,400-6,600 ft that holds established camps; this bench is the last reliable water (small tarns/creek trickle, can run dry by late summer — treat before drinking). From the bench, continue up the main climbers' trail over steep talus and scree to Burgundy Col, which holds three or four bivy sites with old rock wind-shelters built by past parties. From the col, cross to the east side and traverse south over snow and talus at the edge of the Silver Star Glacier basin, below the east walls of Chianti and Pernod. From below the east walls, climb obliquely up and around to the notch between Chianti and Pernod; this section runs to roughly three pitches of mostly 4th and 5th class. Lingering snow on the east side into early July may call for an axe and light traction.
approach_variant_names: The Wine Spires pullout and Burgundy Col, then across the east side to the Pernod–Chianti notch
current.descent: This is a rappel descent, not a walk-off. Rappel from the summit block back to the notch between Pernod and Chianti, then make long rappels down the east side to the snow and névé at the edge of the Silver Star Glacier basin. No rappel count is published for this line; carry double ropes, and cord to back up or replace old slings and bolts. From the glacier edge, traverse back north below Chianti and climb a few hundred feet to regain Burgundy Col, then descend the climbers' trail (scree, the bench, then the timbered rib) to the SR-20 pullout. Watch for moats along the rock late in the season, and budget real time for the loose scree below the col.
current.detailed_rack: Standard alpine rock rack (nuts plus cams to roughly 3 in); given the aid-heavy 1952 first ascent, carry your own gear rather than relying on any old fixed pins or bolts encountered on route.
current.pro_needs: Solid alpine rock pro across the grade.
bivy: Burgundy Col high camp — west side, the Wine Spires
Burgundy Creek bench camp — west side
Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — west side

name: South Route
beta: The standard approach to Phantom Peak uses the Southwest Glacier and South Couloir with a snow ramp at approximately 40-45 degrees. Climbers cross a bergschrund, navigate a steep snow finger, then move onto broken rock with Class 2-3 scrambling before traversing the sharp, exposed summit ridge. The summit consists of solid granitic rock with thrilling exposure on both sides. A hand line or belay may be useful for the narrowest sections.
overview: Phantom Peak is a fittingly named, elusive summit of the Northern Pickets between Fury and the Challenger group, rimming the glacier-draped Luna Cirque. The Southwest Glacier–South Couloir–Southwest Ridge line — the peak's easiest way up (Class 4) — links a pocket glacier, a broken rock step, and a short exposed ridge crest to a summit with a deceptive false summit just below the true top.

current.approach: There are two real approach options for the South (Southwest) Route on Phantom Peak, and both are serious multi-day North Cascades bushwhacks — this is not a trail hike. Option one, the Luna Creek approach: from Ross Lake Resort, take the water taxi across Ross Lake (roughly $35, saves about 6 miles of paddling/road-walking) to the Big Beaver trailhead. From there it's about 9-10 miles of maintained, mostly flat, forested trail up the Big Beaver Creek drainage (through old-growth cedar groves and past beaver ponds/marshy sections) to Luna Camp, an established backcountry campsite where a NOCA wilderness permit is required. From Luna Camp the trail effectively ends; climbers leave the maintained tread and push cross-country up the Luna Creek drainage toward Phantom Peak's south side, gaining roughly 4,000+ ft over a few miles through some of the worst brush in the Cascades. Fred Beckey, on the first traverse through here in 1940, found it a brutal fight through flies, devil's club, willows, and alder — modern parties confirm little has changed, reporting huckleberry, devil's club, vine maple and slide alder so dense that 0.5 mph is a good pace, plus heavy mosquito/fly pressure in summer. The creek itself must be forded in places; fords get harder (deeper, faster) the lower/farther downstream you are, so it's best to gain elevation out of the valley bottom as early as possible rather than fighting the brush along the creek itself. Water is abundant throughout (the creek and countless side-seeps), but hazard is really the terrain: no trail, no cairns, high fall-into-a-hole-in-the-brush risk, and real potential to get separated from a partner in the thick stuff (this has happened to real parties here). Above the brush line the drainage opens into subalpine meadow and talus below Phantom's south aspect. Option two, favored by several recent parties, comes from the north via Whatcom Pass: Hannegan Trailhead (3,100 ft) → Hannegan Pass Trail → Chilliwack River Trail (includes a cable-car creek crossing) → Brush Creek Trail up to Whatcom Pass, then off-trail via the Whatcom Glacier and Perfect Pass to a base camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine. From that camp, the route to Phantom itself is a roughly 1,000-ft descending traverse east across snow/talus to the base of Phantom's broad southwest buttress, then up a snowfield to a saddle around 6,100 ft within the buttress — this saddle is effectively the start of the technical climbing. Whichever approach is used, expect 2-3 days of travel each way.
approach_variant_names: Hannegan Pass, Whatcom Pass and Perfect Pass to a camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine
Big Beaver Trail to Luna Camp, then the Luna Creek bushwhack up Phantom's south side
current.descent: Standard practice is to reverse the ascent line rather than walk off a different way — there is no easy alternate descent gully on this peak. From the true summit, downclimb back across the false-summit ridge crest (using a hand line on the short, exposed step above the false summit if the party fixed one on the way up), then down the broken Class 2-3 rock slope to the top of the snow finger. This is also where you'll retrieve any snow flukes or pickets placed as running protection on the ascent — plan on down-climbing/down-tooling the snow finger and re-crossing the bergschrund via the same slabby rock step used going up. Below the bergschrund, descend the pocket glacier and snowfield back to the ~6,100-ft saddle in the southwest buttress, then reverse the ~1,000-ft traverse back to camp (Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine, if approached from Whatcom Pass) or continue down into the Luna Creek drainage to regain the brush and, eventually, the Big Beaver Trail. The one place real rappelling is recorded on this route is the short, steep summit tower/rock step just below the true summit: the 1959 second-ascent party (Josendal, Sharpe, Spickard) found downclimbing was not comfortable there and made two rappels down a roughly 150-ft cliff band on the east side of the summit ridge to get past it. Given the remote, rarely-visited, and reportedly 'somewhat rotten' rock in this gully/tower section, expect natural anchors only — slung horns or rock threads, not bolts — so carry a small rack of slings/cord for building anchors. A single 60m rope handles the two ~75-ft rappels comfortably (or two 30m/60m ropes if the party prefers not to pull and re-rig). Total descent time from summit back to a southwest-buttress base camp has been reported at around 5-6 hours by a party climbing this line. Overall hazard on descent is exposure and loose rock on the tower/gully sections, plus the same bergschrund and snow-finger objective hazards (crevasse fall, rockfall off the buttress walls) encountered on the way up, and — once back down in the trees — the same brutal, disorienting Luna Creek brush that makes the whole approach infamous.
current.detailed_rack: Minimal gear typically used: selection of nuts (black diamond size range), several slings. No ice screws needed, but 3-4 snow pickets or flukes are required for the snow finger and bergschrund.
rack: Light rack: a few nuts and slings for anchors
Glacier travel kit: rope, crevasse-rescue hardware
current.pro_needs: Snow flukes for bergschrund area and steep slopes. Small emergency kit given remote location and lack of cell service.
bivy: Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine high camp
Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass
Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
current.rope_note: Grade III, Class 4; roped snow/glacier travel with pickets near the bergschrund (~7200ft) transitioning to Class 4 rock on an exposed summit ridge.

name: Standard Scramble
beta: Pinnacle's standard route gains the peak's west-southwest scree-and-talus facade (the gentle side, opposite the precipitous, largely unclimbed east face). Most parties backpack in 9-13 miles through the North Fork Entiat/Snow Brushy Creek drainage to a high basin camp near Saska Pass, then day-trip the summit by dropping into Snow Brushy Creek and climbing to the crest saddle just south of the peak. The final roughly 800 ft to the top is unroped class 2-3 scree and ridge scrambling with no technical climbing; it is very commonly combined with nearby Saska Peak and/or Emerald Peak from the same camp.
overview: Pinnacle Mountain is the high point of a granodiorite/hornblende-quartz-diorite massif (Cardinal Peak pluton) in the Chelan Mountains, a subrange of the Entiat Mountains, within the Glacier Peak Wilderness on the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Entiat Ranger District). At 8,400 ft it is the 4th-highest peak in the Chelan Mountains and the 77th-highest summit in Washington. It is distinct from Pinnacle Peak in the Tatoosh Range near Mount Rainier. First climbed in 1948 by Dwight Watson and Ken Fleming via the south slopes, it drains into both the Entiat and Chelan River watersheds and sees very little traffic thanks to a long, largely off-trail approach through fire-scarred terrain.

current.approach: From the Entiat River/Cottonwood Camp Trailhead, follow the Entiat River Trail roughly 7 miles to the 45-Mile Sheep Driveway, then go off-trail into the Pinnacle Creek drainage toward the south slopes; alternatively, use the North Fork Entiat Trailhead (end of FR 5606, 3,940 ft) and approach from the north side via Trail #1437. Both options require route-finding through 2006/2015 burn areas with heavy deadfall on the lower trail.
approach_variant_names: North Fork Entiat over Saska Pass and Snow Brushy Creek
Entiat River trail and Snow Brushy Creek to Borealis Pass
current.descent: No established alternate descent — down-climb/scree-descend the same south-slopes talus line used on ascent back to the high camp and drainage.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rock rack, rope, or hardware is used on the standard route — it is entirely unroped scrambling.
current.pro_needs: Generally an unroped class 3 scramble; rope optional for the exposed summit block.
bivy: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
Fox Camp, North Fork Entiat trail
current.rope_note: Class 2-3 off-trail ridge/talus scramble from the crest saddle just south of the peak; no rope used on standard route.

name: Pinnacle Saddle / South Gully
beta:
From Pinnacle-Plummer saddle, head east and scramble up obvious gullies on the peak's south side with multiple line options. Stay on most-traveled route for least loose rock. Route-finding is straightforward but exposure increases with altitude. Final push to summit is the steepest and most difficult section, with some variations described as low 5th class.

The usual line is the obvious chute just east of the peak's westernmost rock prominence, about a quarter mile along the boot path from the saddle toward the west side of the south face. Reach it over scree and loose rock along or below the ridge. The chute gets steeper and more exposed as it climbs, but the rock is better cleaned higher up. Protection is limited to a few horns and trees near the top that can be slung, and some parties back off the short top step on one.
overview: Pinnacle Peak (6,562 ft) is the signature summit of the Tatoosh Range and by far the most-climbed peak south of Mount Rainier, thanks to a short, spectacular approach from Reflection Lakes. It is not the range's high point — Unicorn Peak (6,971 ft) holds that distinction — but Pinnacle's central position and classic profile make it the classic Tatoosh outing. (accounts disagree on Pinnacle's exact rank: some listings call it the range's second-highest peak, while NPS materials call it third-highest.) From Pinnacle Saddle (5,920 ft), a loose Class 3-4 scramble up a south-facing gully leads to a summit with close-up views of Rainier's south side and, on clear days, Mount Adams, Mount St. Helens, and Mount Hood.

current.approach: From the Pinnacle Peak Trailhead — a signed, unnumbered NPS trail directly across Stevens Canyon Road from the Reflection Lakes parking pullouts (trailhead elevation ~4,860 ft) — the maintained Pinnacle Saddle Trail climbs at a steady, fairly steep grade through sparse subalpine forest. Around 0.5 mile you get the first partial view of Rainier through the trees; the trail then switchbacks up through subalpine meadow terrain. At about 1.25–1.3 miles and roughly 1,000–1,050 ft of gain you top out at Pinnacle Saddle (~5,900–5,920 ft), the notch between Pinnacle Peak and Plummer Peak, where the maintained trail ends and the view opens south to Mount Adams, St. Helens, and Hood. Carry water from the car — there's no reliable source on the trail or in the gully above except lingering snowmelt early in the season. Past the saddle you leave the maintained tread and the route becomes an unmaintained climbers'/boot path: contour or scramble east into the gully system on the peak's south/southeast face. The rock is old, variable-quality lava flow — solid in spots, rotten in others — so test holds and watch for loose blocks, especially with parties above or below. The gully starts as Class 2 scree and blocky steps, steepening into sustained Class 3 scrambling with real exposure over its upper third, working through a band of trees before a final short scramble to the summit block at 6,562 ft. Snow or verglas can linger in the gully into July on colder years, which turns easy scrambling into a genuine hazard — an ice axe (and willingness to turn around) is worth carrying in early season. Afternoon thunderstorms build quickly over the Tatoosh in summer and this route is fully exposed on an open ridge, so plan to be off the summit by early afternoon.
approach_variant_names: Pinnacle Saddle and the south gully
current.descent: For the standard Class 2–3 scramble, the descent is the same gully used on ascent, back down to Pinnacle Saddle and out the maintained trail to Reflection Lakes — most parties downclimb the whole thing rather than rope up, and this is a walk-off/downclimb route, not a rappel route, in normal summer conditions. That said, the upper gully has a short, sustained Class 3 step with enough exposure that some parties choose to protect or rappel it rather than downclimb, particularly when the rock is wet or in early-season snow: a single ~40 ft rappel off a sling/natural anchor (block, horn, or small cam placement — there is no fixed/bolted anchor) gets you past the crux, after which the remaining scree gully back to the saddle is a straightforward downclimb. Carry a 30m or half a 60m rope and a few slings/small cams if you want this option in your back pocket rather than commit to a sketchy downclimb. Note this is distinct from the separate steeper winter/snow line up the same gully system (climbed with pickets, sometimes 1–2 short roped pitches near the top), which is descended by rappelling the gully on natural gear anchors — that is a different, more technical undertaking than the summer scramble covered here.
current.pro_needs: Rock protection is generally not necessary for the standard route, but scrambling groups should carry light protective gear for emergency use. Rock quality is highly variable due to loose volcanic composition.
bivy: Reflection Lakes area winter snow camp
current.rope_note: Class 3-4 scramble via Pinnacle-Plummer saddle and south gully; loose volcanic rock with exposure - helmet strongly recommended, typically climbed unroped.
